shows.title: Lookout Weekend
shows.description:
The Perez Bros—identical twins Alejandro and Vicente—capture the passion and precision of Los Angeles lowrider culture through painting. This exhibition of new work invites viewers into the garage in the lead-up to a car show or cruise night, featuring scenes of meticulous preparation, tuning, and polishing. The paintings are finished with high-gloss resin and reflective flake, creating a visual surface that mirrors the glossy perfection of the cars themselves and collapses the boundary between subject and medium.

The exhibition title references a 1984 dance track by Debbie Deb that soundtracked the brothers' childhood, setting a tone of hopeful anticipation. While earlier works focus on the cars themselves, this body of work introduces wider scenes, including a panoramic painting of a car show featuring more than a dozen vehicles surrounded by crowds, shade tents, and the bustling community ecosystem that gathers around them. Other works depict cars as near-celebrities, positioned on tow trucks or posed for the camera like stars on a red carpet.

The Perez Bros pull from an extensive photographic archive of the LA lowrider scene, distilling images into scenes of pure detail rendered in bright hues. Their meticulous approach to composition and finish reflects a deep knowledge of and obvious love for the cars and the culture surrounding them—a distinctly Los Angeles subject matter treated with the care of fine art painting.

shows.title: Arreglos Artificiales
shows.description:
Salvador Domínguez opens de boer's fall season with "Arreglos Artificiales" — "artificial arrangements" — a title that plays on the Spanish term for silk-flower bouquets and points toward a practice built on staged, synthetic tableaux. Domínguez, an LA-based painter, works in a hyper-saturated, faintly surreal figurative mode, often placing solitary or paired figures inside interiors thick with pattern, drapery, and decorative objects that feel simultaneously domestic and theatrical.

Based on the works available ahead of the opening, the show looks to continue his interest in the artifice of everyday staging — flowers that don't wilt, rooms arranged for effect rather than comfort — using it as a lens on inherited Latino domestic aesthetics and the performance of hospitality and care. It's a promising follow-up slot after the gallery's summer run of Kash Ford, and a chance to catch an emerging painter's work in a single, focused presentation before the fall art-fair circuit picks up.

venue.name: de boer
venue.address: 3311 E Pico Blvd, Los Angeles, CA 90023

shows.title: GREMLIN: Museum of Commerce
shows.description:
Nick Herman has spent two decades making sculpture, photography, and books that treat industrial materials and structural systems as raw poetic material — fat solids cast into a lunar-looking frieze, hand-tied nets that sag under their own logic, antennas that double as myth machines. Museum of Commerce, his solo turn at FOYER-LA titled GREMLIN, promises more of that same sleight of hand: taking the leftover vocabulary of manufacturing, retail, and technology and bending it toward something stranger and more bodily.

FOYER-LA is exactly the kind of space this work needs. Herman's MFA is in sculpture from Yale, and his exhibition history runs through Socrates Sculpture Park, LAXART, and the Chinati Foundation's collection, so a project-space outing lets him work at a scale and speed that bigger institutions don't allow.

Given the title's nod to commerce and gremlins alike, expect a show that pokes at consumer culture and the "traumatic residue" — Herman's own phrase — that industry and technology leave on both land and body. It's a compact, single-artist project, which makes it an easy, quick stop for anyone curious about one of LA's more understated sculptor-writers.

shows.title: Vestiges
shows.description:
Alexandra Lopez Iglesias works in paper and clay, two materials she treats less as substances to be shaped than as stand-ins for skin — things that absorb, scar, and record whatever touches them. Vestiges, her solo show at Keystone Art Space, is built from sculptures that use cutting, piercing, tearing, stitching, and scraping to leave visible traces of contact on their surfaces, insisting throughout that these forms aren't metaphors for bodies so much as bodies themselves.

Lopez Iglesias, who was born in Ciudad Juárez and now works in Los Angeles, has built her practice around a fascination with materiality that reportedly goes back to childhood — an early, almost compulsive attention to the textures of the built world around her. That sensitivity to surface and touch carries through into paper especially, a medium she has also taught as a papermaking process in academic settings, giving her sculptures an unusual technical rigor beneath their raw, worked-over look.

The show takes place in Keystone Art Space's daylit gallery inside the artist-studio complex in Lincoln Heights — a fitting context for work that's this tactile and process-driven. It's a short run, just over a week, so this is very much a catch-it-while-you-can show for anyone interested in sculpture that treats the body's history of being touched, held, or neglected as its actual subject matter.

shows.title: Charles Dickson: Select Works, 1966-2026
shows.description:
Charles Dickson has been carving since he was five years old, whittling toy knives under the blankets in South Central Los Angeles, and this survey at Parrasch Heijnen compresses sixty years of that practice into one gallery. Select Works, 1966-2026 pulls from across his career — wood, bronze, concrete, metal, glass, acrylic — tracking a self-taught sculptor who came up alongside Noah Purifoy and John Outterbridge in the Watts arts scene of the late 1960s and never really left it, becoming the longtime artist-in-residence at the Watts Towers Arts Center and groundskeeper of the Towers themselves.

What unites the wildly different materials in Dickson's work is a consistent visual language drawn from African sculptural tradition — masks, totemic forms, ritual tools — repurposed to catalog and honor Black life and history in Los Angeles specifically. He's best known publicly for civic commissions like the Mariposa Metro Green Line station and the Martin Luther King Jr. memorial in Watts, but this gallery presentation gets at the more intimate, studio-based side of his output: carved reliefs, assemblages, and figures that read like a private notebook kept over six decades.

A show spanning 1966 to 2026 is essentially a mini-retrospective, and it's a notable get for a Boyle Heights gallery to present a Los Angeles art-world elder statesman whose work usually turns up in museums and public plazas rather than commercial spaces. Worth seeing both for the sculpture itself and as a rare chance to see this much of Dickson's range in one room.

shows.title: All Unfinished
shows.description:
Nic Gregory's solo show at ace/121 Gallery takes its title from a state most artists know intimately: the not-quite-resolved painting, the piece that keeps changing hands between finished and in-progress. Working in acrylic on wood panel, Gregory builds surfaces with a rough, worked-over quality — visible layering, exposed grain, and passages that look deliberately left raw alongside more resolved sections.

The result is painting that treats incompleteness as subject matter rather than a flaw to be corrected, asking viewers to consider process and provisionality as part of the finished object. It's a fitting complement to ace/121's program, which Glendale Arts uses to spotlight Los Angeles-based painters and sculptors in an intimate, artist-colony setting.

This is the gallery's first exhibition of its fall season, opening in late September after a summer show by Leah Knecht, and it continues ace/121's pattern of tightly focused, single-artist presentations that give each body of work room to breathe in the gallery's modest footprint.

shows.title: Artifacts from an Unborn Empire
shows.description:
Timed to land on the 250th anniversary of the United States, this group exhibition turns a skeptical eye on the myths nations tell about their own founding. Curators Jason Jenn and Vojislav Radovanović have assembled more than twenty Los Angeles-based artists — including Ben Cuevas, Elana Mann, Gina Herrera, Rubén Esparza, Kristine Schomaker, and Marcus Kuiland-Nazario — working across knit sculpture, ceramics, photography, installation, and performance documentation to ask who gets to write history and whose symbols survive it.

The work on view ranges from intimate to spectacular: a skull knitted from acrylic yarn, hand-drawn maps of imagined cities labeled in overlapping languages, a nude fiberglass figure inked in dark patterns, and an installation of clear crystalline forms suspended over a hardwood floor. Photographic documentation of performance and costume work — including a startling image of a performer under a stoplight in an Elizabethan gown built from egg cartons — sits alongside spray-painted text works and painted wood assemblages, giving the show a restless, materially inventive feel.

Brand Library & Art Center's gallery, a light-filled space attached to a public library devoted to art and music, has a long history of hosting ambitious, community-minded group shows, and this one continues that tradition by pairing serious conceptual ambition with genuine visual variety. It's a fitting way to mark a fraught national anniversary — not with celebration, but with inquiry into empire, colonial legacy, and the stories a culture chooses to keep.

shows.title: Fantasy Street / The Lifted Veil
shows.description:
Milano Chow's site-specific installation takes over a small, historically layered room inside Hollyhock House — once a child's bedroom, later a clubhouse lounge — with folding screens of graphite, ink, and photo-transfer drawings. Her invented facades borrow the vocabulary of 1920s Los Angeles (movie palaces, apartment blocks, shop windows pulled from the public library's photo archive) to build streetscapes that look documentary but exist nowhere, a fitting echo of Frank Lloyd Wright's own fabricated ornament just outside the door.

Alongside her own work, Chow has curated a companion exhibition of photographs by the late Deborah Turbeville, the fashion photographer known for hazy, fractured images that unsettled the glossy conventions of Vogue and Harper's Bazaar. The pairing sets Chow's crisp, monochrome invented architecture against Turbeville's blurred, deteriorated interiors and contact-sheet outtakes, both artists drawn to environments that feel staged, aged, or slightly unreal.

It's a smart, quiet two-hander for a house that has spent a century blurring the line between architecture and stage set — Wright designed Hollyhock House as a kind of total artwork for Aline Barnsdall, and successive artist interventions here have leaned into that theatricality. Worth the trip for anyone who wants to see contemporary drawing and vintage fashion photography in conversation inside one of LA's few UNESCO World Heritage sites, rather than in a white-box gallery.

shows.title: Revington Arthur: A Retrospective
shows.description:
Beverly Art Boutique's standing exhibition gathers work spanning the long career of Revington Arthur (1908–1986), an American painter, educator, and print-world organizer who trained at the Art Students League under teachers including Arshile Gorky and George Luks. The gallery draws on a large estate holding of more than 700 original works, letting visitors trace Arthur's evolution from nature studies and figurative American-scene painting toward the hard-edged, primary-colored geometric abstraction he developed in the 1950s and after, much of it inflected by the era's fascination with space travel and technology.

What's on the walls ranges from early lyrical landscapes and lifestyle scenes to the later non-objective compositions built from interlocking geometric shapes — canvases that read as a personal register of mid-century American formal experimentation, made by a painter who spent decades teaching as much as exhibiting. Arthur also founded the Chautauqua Art Center and co-founded the New England and National Print Show, and his paintings entered the collections of institutions such as the Brooklyn Museum, the Walker Art Center, and the Albright-Knox (now Buffalo AKG).

This is a small, retail-adjacent gallery rather than a curated museum show, but it functions as an accessible, walk-in survey of an under-recognized figure whose geometric abstractions are otherwise scattered across regional museum vaults and auction houses. Worth a stop for anyone curious about the lesser-known corners of postwar American abstraction, especially the pieces where Arthur's Cold War-era geometric language is at its most confident.

shows.title: the sound i saw
shows.description:
Roy DeCarava spent the late 1940s through the 1960s photographing New York City's Black life with an eye tuned as much to sound as to sight, and this exhibition — curated by Ebony L. Haynes — reassembles the body of work he called the sound i saw. First put together as a handmade artist's book and later shown at the Studio Museum in Harlem in 1983, the project weaves images of jazz musicians on and off stage with pictures of everyday street life: deliverymen, kids playing, commuters waiting on a platform. DeCarava's silver gelatin prints are famous for their deep, controlled tonality, and the pairing of music-adjacent and street imagery is his way of asking viewers to notice the rhythm and improvisation already present in ordinary city life.

David Zwirner is pairing the photographs with a listening room built around DeCarava's own jazz record collection and playlists, an unusual curatorial move that leans into the show's audio-visual premise rather than just gesturing at it.

DeCarava's history in Los Angeles is thin, which is part of what makes this show notable: the gallery notes it's only the fourth time his work has been shown solo in the city, after a 1982 appearance at the Los Angeles Center for Photographic Studies, LACMA's 1996 retrospective, and a 2019 show at the Underground Museum. For a photographer this influential, that's a striking scarcity, and reason enough to make time for it.

shows.title: Global Fugitivity: UCLA New Wight International Biennial Exhibition 2026
shows.description:
Every two years, UCLA's graduate art students curate the New Wight Biennial by traveling to studio programs around the world and selecting work from a rising generation of MFA candidates. This edition, organized by student-curators Sabaah Folayan, tunmi da silva, and Luke Francis Austin, takes "fugitivity" as its theme — art-world shorthand for practices of escape, refusal, and self-determination that run through Black studies and diaspora theory.

Expect a wide-ranging, multimedia group show: the biennial has historically mixed painting, video, sculpture, and installation from art schools across North America and abroad, giving Los Angeles audiences an early look at artists who haven't yet had gallery representation. Because it's juried through studio visits rather than an open submission, the show tends to have a sharper, more considered feel than a typical student exhibition.

The New Wight Gallery is a teaching space as much as an exhibition venue, tucked into the ground floor of the Broad Art Center just north of the Murphy Sculpture Garden, and this biennial is one of the few times each cycle that its program looks outward past UCLA's own graduate cohort.

shows.title: Form Follows Feeling
shows.description:
Oliver Lee Jackson has spent six decades building paintings and sculptures around the human figure, and this show — Lisson's first with the Oakland-based artist at its Los Angeles space — brings together work from across that span rather than presenting a single recent series. Paintings built from spraypaint, chalk, enamel and oil stick sit alongside a rarer body of work: carved marble and mixed-media sculptures, some begun decades ago in Carrara and only now completed, that Jackson treats as slow accumulations of cloth, graphite, gold leaf and stone.

What ties the two mediums together is Jackson's refusal to let the figure resolve into simple likeness. Bodies appear crouched, in flight, or dissolving into their colored grounds, which are prepared for him by assistants without his knowledge beforehand, forcing an element of chance into every composition. The sculptures work similarly by accretion, with fresh material grafted onto old fragments so that a single totemic form can carry the residue of years of studio time.

It's a useful corrective for anyone who knows Jackson mainly through museum surveys at the National Gallery or the Saint Louis Art Museum: here the sculptural side of his practice, last seen publicly in a 2024 High Line commission, gets real room to breathe alongside the paintings that made his reputation.

shows.title: Hard Line Women
shows.description:
Nonaka-Hill gathers twelve Japanese women artists — among them Atsuko Tanaka, Rei Kawakubo, Kazuko Miyamoto, Tomie Ohtake and Kay Sekimachi — who each, at some point across six decades, worked in a hard-edged, geometric vocabulary that had little patience for softness or sentiment. The show spans painting, sculpture, textile, performance documentation and photography, and its animating idea is straightforward but rarely stated this plainly: that rigor and coolness were themselves a form of resistance for these artists, a way of working against the expressive, macho postures that dominated so much postwar art criticism.

Several of the artists included — Eiko Yamazawa, Aiko Miyawaki, Etsuko Nakatsuji, Shizuko Yoshikawa — also worked as graphic designers, and the show argues that this dual practice sharpened rather than diluted their formal thinking, feeding a shared interest in order and non-psychological composition. Pairing canonical names like Tanaka with far less exhibited figures like Sumie Aoki and Akiko Horio should make for a genuinely instructive walk through twentieth-century Japanese abstraction.

shows.title: Book of Sand
shows.description:
Elliott Hundley's seventh solo show with Regen Projects trades the Greek tragedies and Rilke sonnets that anchored his earlier bodies of work for something more interior. Book of Sand — titled after the Borges story about an infinite, unreadable book — takes its structural cue from Jungian sand-tray therapy, in which patients arrange miniature figures in sand to surface unconscious material. Several paintings here are bordered like a sand tray itself, turning the gallery into a kind of psychic stage where Hundley's signature accumulations of paper, pins, string and encaustic play the role of figurines.

The show's centerpiece sculptures continue Hundley's practice of building around personally resonant found objects: Palette (2024) fuses concrete, bone, rattan, feathers and other studio detritus into a totem-like column, while a large tapestry incorporates fabric from his mother's wedding veil. It's dense, accretive work that rewards close looking rather than a quick pass, consistent with an artist who trained at UCLA and has had museum surveys at the Nasher Sculpture Center, the Wexner Center and, most recently, the Santa Barbara Museum of Art.

Running concurrently in the gallery's viewing rooms is a focused selection of small watercolor-on-canvas paintings and studies by the late Silke Otto-Knapp (1970–2022), a former UCLA painting professor whose grayscale "erasure" technique — layering and scraping black watercolor to let a white ground emerge — offers a quieter, more austere counterpoint to Hundley's maximalism just steps away.

shows.title: Control X
shows.description:
Tala Madani returns to her longtime Los Angeles gallery with a new suite of paintings and video animation that continues her interrogation of power, bodies, and the slippery line between creation and destruction. The Iranian-born, LA-based artist has built her reputation on a scabrous, funny, and often unsettling cartoon language, using loose brushwork and simplified male figures to needle at authority, shame, and domestic absurdity. This show pushes that language into new territory with a series of "mountain portraits" that swell human subjects into landscape-scale forms, riffing on the grandiosity of Romantic painting while still handling paint with an intimate, almost bodily touch.

The centerpiece is reportedly Madani's most ambitious video to date, an animated work built from painted, drawn, and photographed source material and scored by artist Nathaniel Mellors, in which renegade letters of the alphabet escape the page and start remaking the world in their own image — a fable about language, domination, and the way symbols calcify into systems of control. It's a natural extension of Madani's long-running interest in animation as a sibling practice to her paintings, and it gives the show its title's double meaning: control as command, and "X" as erasure.

Madani has had a genuinely international decade, with solo museum shows at MOCA Los Angeles, the Mori Art Museum, Secession Vienna, and most recently the Henry Art Gallery in Seattle, plus inclusion in the Istanbul and Whitney Biennials. Seeing new work in her home city, in the gallery that has represented her for years, is a chance to track an artist still actively complicating a visual vocabulary that has already become widely influential.

shows.title: Who Needs Muscles If Nothing Is Heavy?
shows.description:
Bridget Mullen's fourth solo show with the gallery gathers fifteen paintings built around the idea of mutation: a shape or gesture in one canvas warps, migrates, and resurfaces transformed in the next, like a visual game of telephone. Hands grip empty sleeves, bulging eyes press against intestinal grids, and a figure descends a staircase split awkwardly across two abutting canvases — the seams and staggered panels are as much the subject as the imagery itself.

Mullen works without preliminary sketches, letting abstract marks and negative space calcify into figures and structures as she paints, so the pictures read as records of perception catching up with itself. That process gives the show its philosophical undertow (there are nods to Merleau-Ponty's idea that sensation is inseparable from the body doing the sensing) without ever feeling like an illustrated thesis; the paintings are strange, funny, and viscerally alive with pattern, hair, brick, and plumbing standing in for the membranes between inside and outside, body and object.

Mullen has had a serious decade of momentum — residencies at Skowhegan, MacDowell, and Yaddo, a Headlands Chiaro Award, and work now held by the Museum Boijmans Van Beuningen and other institutions — and this exhibition, her most ambitious presentation of new work in Los Angeles yet, is a good chance to see how her language keeps mutating in real time.

shows.title: Desert Lenses
shows.description:
Ry Rocklen has spent years turning cast-off household objects into ceramic sculpture, and Desert Lenses points that habit of attention out toward the high desert. The show's title works as a pun: everyday things we can't do without — a sock, a slice of toast, a strip of Venetian blind — are recast in glazed ceramic using mold-making and photographic transfer, so that a mundane object becomes a kind of viewing device, a lens onto the wider landscape around it.

The "Absorption Panel" series is the clearest expression of that idea: flat ceramic panels bearing photo-real images of bread, candy, or a window pressed into three-dimensional relief, blurring the line between picture and object. Elsewhere, socks hang like curtains and everyday debris gets the reverent, slightly absurd treatment of a still-life painting. Rocklen has a long history of finding grandeur in domestic detritus — trophies made from furniture, shelving built from personal effects — and this show extends that sensibility into the wide-open, sun-bleached terrain of the Mojave and beyond, treating the desert less as scenery than as a mood that seeps into ordinary objects.

It's a show that rewards close looking: the ceramics photograph well but read very differently in person, where the glaze catches light and the illusion of photographic flatness gives way to the material reality of clay.

shows.title: 2026 K-Comics Origin Los Angeles: Korean Webtoon Experience Exhibition
shows.description:
This is less a gallery show than a walk-through pop-culture pavilion: the Korean Creative Content Agency and KCCLA have turned the center's second-floor art gallery into an immersive tribute to Korean webtoons, tracing roughly a century of Korean comics up through the digital-native "webtoon" format that now drives some of the biggest entertainment franchises on the planet.

Three hit series anchor the installation — All of Us Are Dead, Omniscient Reader's Viewpoint, and Solo Leveling — with large-scale graphic environments, character models, and interactive stations built around each. Rather than framing panels on a wall, the show leans into spatial installation and role-play: visitors move through recreated sets and photo-ready tableaux that translate a scrolling digital medium into a physical, room-sized experience.

It's a useful reminder that Koreatown's cultural institutions treat comics and animation as part of the same continuum as painting and calligraphy, and it's a rare chance to see original character and production art from webtoons that mostly live on phone screens blown up to mural scale. Free admission and no reservation required make it an easy add to a Wilshire museum-row afternoon.

shows.title: Tacita Dean: FILM
shows.description:
Marciano reopens after its summer install break with the U.S. debut of one of Tacita Dean's signature works: FILM, an 11-minute, silent 35mm installation originally commissioned by Tate Modern for its Turbine Hall in 2011. Dean projects the piece onto a vertical screen so that a strip of film seems to rise straight up out of the gallery floor, sprocket holes and all, turning the physical apparatus of analog cinema into the actual subject of the image.

Inside that towering frame, Dean intercuts a private visual vocabulary — a waterfall, a street clock, a pine tree, an ostrich egg, a flickering bulb — with glimpses of the Turbine Hall's industrial architecture, using century-old in-camera tricks like glass matte painting and multiple exposure rather than digital effects. It's a monument to photochemical film built at a moment when the medium's survival was genuinely in question, and Dean has said as much herself: her practice treats celluloid as something closer to poetry than to mere image-capture.

Seeing FILM at Marciano also means seeing the building itself, a former Scottish Rite Masonic temple that gives the piece's monolithic verticality an unusually theatrical setting. The show opens alongside Pierre Leguillon's Ads & Brands and continues Marciano's rotation of collection-based and single-artist installations throughout its Wilshire Boulevard galleries.

shows.title: Flesh Witness
shows.artist: Bernice Akamine, Lani Asunción, Pelenakeke Brown, Crystal Z Campbell, Jisoo Chung, Sean Connelly, Kyuri Jeon, Jane Jin Kaisen, Mao Ishikawa, Slow Futures Laboratory, Stephanie Syjuco
shows.description:
Flesh Witness gathers eleven artists and collectives working across Hawai'i, Korea, Okinawa, the Philippines, and Samoa to trace how militarism has been written onto bodies, landscapes, and official archives over the past half-century. The show's title borrows from Kyuri Jeon's video piece about Korean War prisoners who were forcibly tattooed with anti-communist slogans, and that image of skin as a site of imposed history sets the tone for everything around it: photographs and film stills pulled from state archives, sculpture built from coastal materials, and new commissions that talk back to that archival record.

Organized by the diasporic Korean arts nonprofit GYOPO with scholar Amy Kahng, the exhibition spans works from the 1970s to newly commissioned pieces, including a still from Jane Jin Kaisen's film "Burial of This Order" and photography by Mao Ishikawa documenting Okinawa under US occupation. Rather than treating these histories as separate national stories, the curators line them up so the shared machinery of occupation and control becomes visible across very different Pacific and Asian geographies.

It's the kind of ambitious, research-driven group show REDCAT's gallery does well: free to enter, modest in scale, but dense with material that rewards slow looking. The opening reception on September 12 kicks off a run through mid-December, giving plenty of time to catch it alongside the fall performance season upstairs.

shows.title: Sit So Your Back Isn't Against The Door
shows.description:
This is the rarely-seen, most unguarded corner of Glenn Ligon's practice: his Coloring Book paintings, made after a 1999-2000 residency at the Walker Art Center where he handed out pages from Afrocentric coloring books of the late 1960s and '70s and let children scribble on them. Ligon then blew those uninhibited marks up into large-scale canvases, turning a kid's crayon work into paintings about authorship, historical memory, and who gets to narrate Black history and iconography. The bright, candy-colored surfaces read as pure fun before the harder questions underneath start to surface.

Ligon is best known for his text paintings built from James Baldwin and Zora Neale Hurston quotations, so this body of work shows a different, more collaborative and improvisational side of an artist who has spent four decades picking apart how American language and imagery encode race. The show marks the first time these paintings have been reunited in over 25 years, which alone makes it a significant occasion for anyone who has followed his career since his 2011 Whitney retrospective "AMERICA."

The exhibition opens the gallery's fall season alongside Jack Whitten's "The Numinous," reopening the Downtown LA campus after a period of installation and marking ten years since Hauser & Wirth first arrived in the Arts District. Entry is free and no booking is required.

shows.title: Carl Cheng: Nature Never Loses
shows.description:
Carl Cheng has been quietly making some of Los Angeles's most prescient art since the 1960s, and this survey — the first to trace his full six-decade career — finally gives him the wide-lens treatment. Cheng trained in both fine art and industrial design, and it shows: his work looks like it was made by an engineer moonlighting as a conceptualist, full of erosion machines, simulated landscapes, plastic "nature" specimens, and gadgets that turn ecological anxiety into something you can crank a handle to operate. Coming out of the aerospace-saturated, politically charged Los Angeles of the 1960s and 70s, he became one of the sharpest artists anywhere on the subject of humans trying (and failing) to engineer their way around nature.

The show, organized by The Contemporary Austin and previously seen at ICA Philadelphia, Bonnefanten, and Museum Tinguely, lands at ICA LA as the final stop on its international tour — fittingly, since Cheng has lived and worked in Santa Monica for most of his career and showed at the museum's predecessor, the Santa Monica Museum of Art, back in 1998. Expect around fifty works and archival materials, including his signature "erosion machines" that use pebbles, water pumps and black light to simulate geological time in real time, plus a new water-based commission made specifically for this presentation.

Paired in the same season with Amia Yokoyama's first institutional solo show in the Project Room and a new Zoe Walsh mural on the building's 7th Street façade, this is ICA LA's strongest fall lineup in some time — a chance to see an underrated LA original get his due alongside two much younger artists extending some of the same questions about bodies, technology and land.

venue.name: Institute of Contemporary Art, Los Angeles (ICA LA)

shows.title: Healing with Gold: The Art of Kintsugi on Ceramics & Beyond
shows.description:
Kintsugi — the practice of repairing broken ceramics with gold-dusted lacquer — has become such a popular metaphor in wellness culture that it's easy to forget the actual objects behind it: centuries-old tea bowls whose cracks were mended rather than hidden, turning damage into ornament. This group show at JACCC's Doizaki Gallery, curated by Japanese art historian Meher McArthur, puts those historical vessels in the same room as more than thirty contemporary works that take the kintsugi philosophy in far more varied directions.

The exhibition is organized in three parts, moving from the traditional tea-ceremony roots of gold lacquer repair through contemporary artists actively practicing the technique on ceramics, and finally to work that borrows kintsugi's logic — visible repair as a form of beauty — for painting, sculpture, textile art and installation. Artists in the show include Miya Ando, Naoko Fukumaru, Ted Meyer and Kristine Schomaker, among others, several of whom have used the idea of "golden repair" to address illness, grief, or trauma rather than literal broken pottery.

It's a modest but well-considered survey of an idea that gets invoked constantly and examined rarely — a chance to see where the actual craft tradition ends and the metaphor begins, all inside a 2,000-square-foot gallery in the heart of Little Tokyo. An opening reception and a curator's tour the following weekend offer two easy ways to catch McArthur's thinking on the show in person.

venue.name: Japanese American Cultural & Community Center (JACCC) – George J. Doizaki Gallery

shows.title: Into the Lake of Fire // ⲉ̀ϧⲟⲩⲛ ⲉ̀ϯⲗⲩⲙⲛⲏ ⲛ̀ⲭ̀ⲣⲱⲙ
shows.description:
Sherin Guirguis returns to Luis De Jesus with a suite of monoprints made during a Sam Francis Foundation fellowship in Paris, where she worked directly with Egyptian heritage objects held in French institutions. The prints use gold, faience blue, carnelian red, and ochre — pigments drawn from Egyptian art and architecture — layered on black paper so that glyphs and ritual patterns seem to float or dissolve into the surface. It's quiet, research-driven work that turns museum archives into a starting point for something personal rather than an ending point.

The title nods to a passage from the ancient funerary text long mistranslated as "The Book of the Dead," and the whole project is really about translation and mistranslation: how colonial-era archaeology flattened and renamed Indigenous Egyptian (RemenKeemi) culture, and what it looks like to work back through that record toward something closer to the original meaning. Repetition — printmaking's basic gesture — becomes a way of insisting on memory against erasure.

Guirguis is an LA-based, Cairo-born artist whose work sits in the collections of LACMA and MOCA, among others, and who has built large-scale public commissions from the Pyramids of Giza to Desert X. This is smaller, more intimate work than those outdoor pieces, made for close looking, and it rewards it — the surfaces have a jeweled, light-catching quality that's hard to get across in photos.

shows.title: Camino y Paz
shows.description:
Ángeles Agrela paints and draws women whose faces are all but consumed by cascades of hair — thick, colorful, sculptural masses rendered in acrylic and pencil on paper at a scale that turns portraiture into something closer to landscape. The Granada-based Spanish artist has spent years using hair as her central subject, treating it as a stand-in for the layered, often contradictory ways femininity has been depicted across art history, from Pre-Raphaelite muses to contemporary fashion imagery.

Camino y Paz gathers new large-scale works, many nearly six feet tall, each built around a pair or single sitter whose identity is partly obscured by an exuberant tangle of pattern and color. The effect is playful but pointed: by hiding the face, the traditional site of a portrait's meaning, Agrela redirects attention to costume, gesture, and the sheer physical presence of hair as material and metaphor.

This is Agrela's first solo exhibition at Nicodim's Los Angeles space, following her inclusion in the gallery's group shows over the past several years and solo presentations in New York, Marbella, and Vancouver. Her work sits in public collections including CAC Málaga and the National Library of Spain, and this show extends a body of work that has been steadily gaining international attention.

shows.title: Happy Trails
shows.description:
Sarah Miska paints horses and the people who work with them, and for her third solo show at Night Gallery she trades the English riding world of her earlier paintings for the American West. Last fall she spent six weeks painting out of a converted horse stable in Wyoming, and the resulting canvases draw on photographs she took there — cattle ranches, working horses, and the wranglers and apprentices who tend them.

The paintings are meticulous in a way that rewards close looking: individual strands of mane, the sheen of a cow's ear in the sun, the particular sun-bleached texture of denim and leather. Miska has always been interested in the intimacy between horse and rider, and here she extends that interest to the practical, unglamorous labor of ranch life — a deliberate departure from the tailored, aristocratic associations of the equestrian paintings that made her name.

What holds the show together is Miska's refusal to let Western and equestrian subject matter sit at the margins of "serious" painting. Her sculptural training shows in how she handles bodies and space, and the paintings have a voyeuristic closeness that turns grooming rituals and rough terrain into meditations on self-presentation and control.

shows.title: Future Past Tense
shows.artist: Esperanza Cortés, Cheryl Derricotte, Karen Hampton, Asa Jackson, Fay Ku
shows.description:
Future Past Tense brings together five artists — Esperanza Cortés, Cheryl Derricotte, Karen Hampton, Asa Jackson, and Fay Ku — whose work treats personal and historical memory as material to be woven, cast, or dyed rather than simply narrated. The show spans tapestry, kiln-formed glass, beaded and clay sculpture, and graphite drawing, but the artists share a habit of using craft traditions to carry difficult inherited histories forward.

Karen Hampton's indigo tapestries grew out of a visit to the South Carolina plantation that gave her family its surname, and Asa Jackson's monumental woven pieces reference the indigo-dyed cotton once worn by enslaved laborers. Cheryl Derricotte's glass "books" with invented titles quietly needle at the erasure of Black women from professional and historical record, while Esperanza Cortés's beaded and clay sculptures draw on the folk-art and ritual traditions of the Americas to push back against colonial narratives. Fay Ku's graphite and watercolor drawings, rooted in the fables her family told after emigrating from Taiwan, add a more intimate, fantastical register to the show.

Individually, several of these artists have exhibition histories with major institutions — Hampton's work sits in the Museum of Fine Arts Boston and the Denver Art Museum, and Cortés has a concurrent show opening at New York's Hispanic Society Museum & Library this September. Together at Patricia Sweetow, their work makes a quiet case that craft media are especially suited to holding onto histories that official records tend to smooth over.

shows.title: Dead Relatives
shows.description:
Superchief Gallery's Halloween-season group show rounds up more than 80 artists working in tattoo flash, lowrider culture, punk photography, printmaking, oil painting, airbrush and graffiti for a three-week run timed to close on Halloween itself. Expect the gallery's usual maximalist hang — walls packed salon-style, multiple murals, and a run of pop-up events throughout October rather than a single quiet opening.

The work leans hard into outlaw and underground iconography: skulls, saints, lowrider pinstriping, anarchist slogans and DIY punk ephemera show up across paintings, prints and mixed-media pieces from artists like Bradley Riot, Monte, Andrew Murga and Oscar Rodriguez. It's less a curated thesis show than a communal gathering of LA's tattoo, street-art and DIY scenes, in keeping with Superchief's long-running mission of building a scrappy, anti-elitist alternative to the gallery mainstream.

Superchief has spent over a decade cultivating exactly this kind of crowd — accessible price points, a rotating cast of emerging and outsider artists, and a calendar built around themed group shows rather than solo museum-style presentations. Dead Relatives fits that mold: a loud, dense, unapologetically populist show best experienced in person during one of its October events.

shows.title: Thomas Demand
shows.description:
Thomas Demand builds his photographs before he ever picks up a camera. The German artist recreates scenes from memory, media images, or historical objects entirely out of paper and cardboard, photographs the fragile constructions under exacting studio light, and then destroys them — so the print is the only trace of the sculpture that made it. This new body of work turns to the miniature theater: eighteenth- and nineteenth-century opera and ballet set models held in museum collections in Vienna, Monaco, and Munich, originally built for productions of Wagner's Tannhäuser and Rossini's Guillaume Tell. Demand photographed these tiny stages with a periscope threaded into their interiors, turning toy-sized scenography into images of genuine theatrical scale and shadow.

Alongside the model photographs, the show includes newer images of Demand's own invented tableaux — an overstuffed bookshelf, reeds catching light on a pond's surface — printed directly onto copper sheets, a material choice that nods back to Renaissance panel painting and early printmaking. It's a quieter, more intimate register for an artist best known for reconstructing scenes of political and historical consequence.

Demand's photographs sit in the collections of MoMA and the Neue Nationalgalerie, and he represented Germany at the São Paulo Bienal in 2004; a related survey of this same body of work, "Rooms That Dream of the Past," is currently on view at Vienna's MAK museum. Seeing the Los Angeles show alongside that context underscores how deliberately Demand blurs the line between document and fabrication — every image here looks like straightforward reportage until you remember that none of what's pictured actually exists anymore.

shows.title: worthless serpentine
shows.description:
Marley Freeman builds her paintings the way a weaver builds cloth: layer by layer, thread of color over thread of color, until an image emerges that feels less composed than grown. For "worthless serpentine," her latest solo show at Parker Gallery, she brings a new group of canvases that continue her long study of abstraction rooted in the structure of textiles — warp and weft translated into hand-mixed gesso and shifting fields of oil and acrylic.

Freeman's forms hover at the edge of recognition: biomorphic shapes, loose grids, and soft-edged color blocks that seem to pulse against one another rather than sit still. The paintings reward slow looking, the kind you'd give a piece of fabric held up to the light — noticing where colors bleed into their neighbors and where a hard edge suddenly appears. It's intimate, handmade work, made by an artist whose paintings already hang in the collections of LACMA and the Hammer.

Freeman — based between New York and Massachusetts but deeply tied to the gallery's history (this is her fourth solo show there since 2018) — continues to develop the language she's built over years of showing with Parker. This show is a good chance to see how her work has evolved since her last outing here in 2023.

shows.title: A Human Pace
shows.description:
Paolo Ventura builds miniature worlds and then photographs them as though they were full-scale film sets, and A Human Pace finds him turning that method toward Paris. His pictures conjure a city suspended between memory and invention: deserted streets, lone figures under streetlamps, and interiors that feel like stage sets abandoned mid-scene. The mood is melancholic and theatrical rather than documentary — this is a Paris assembled from nostalgia and imagination as much as from observation.

Ventura, an Italian photographer known for meticulously constructed dioramas populated with handmade figures, has built a career on blurring the line between staged fiction and lived history, and this body of work continues that practice at a more intimate, human scale.

For viewers who know Ventura's earlier war-haunted tableaux, A Human Pace is a gentler register — closer to reverie than reckoning — but it retains his signature patience: every shadow and prop placed with the deliberateness of a diorama-builder rather than a street photographer.

shows.title: our sharp line of sight
shows.description:
Fabiola Menchelli works without a camera, using photosensitive paper and light itself as raw material to build images that sit somewhere between photograph, sculpture and painting. For her third solo show at Marshall Gallery, the Mexico City-based artist turns exclusively to the prismatic, camera-less chromogenic prints that have dominated her practice over the past two years, folding each of two dozen unique works into a custom color-matched shadowbox frame.

The presentation borrows its atmosphere from Menchelli's 2024–25 museum show at the Norton Museum of Art, with dimly lit, magenta-hued walls meant to intensify the saturated color fields in the work. Titles like "green supercell" and "fire wire" point to the elemental, almost meteorological quality of her abstractions — fields of color that read as light caught mid-event rather than fixed on paper.

Menchelli has spent over a decade investigating what a photograph can be once you remove the lens, and this exhibition arrives at a moment of wider institutional attention to her work, including a recent Getty Museum acquisition from her Queer Horizons series. Seeing two dozen of these intimate, glowing objects together in one room is a rare chance to watch a single idea — light as material — worked through in quiet, obsessive variation.
shows.reception: Opening reception with the artist: Friday, September 11, 2026, 5:00-8:00 pm

shows.title: William Carson
shows.description:
William Carson paints with a geologist's patience, building his abstract compositions out of dense, mineral-like layers of pigment that recall banded rock, weathered stone and the slow accretion of sediment. This solo show at Nüart's Bergamot Station location gathers new paintings that continue his long-running conversation between geological process and human perception — surfaces that look excavated as much as painted.

Carson has shown with Nüart across both its Santa Monica and Santa Fe locations for years, including a recent two-person pairing with Emilio Lobato earlier this year. This solo outing gives his work room to breathe, letting the shifts in his palette — from warm ochres to cooler veins of white and grey — read as a kind of visual stratigraphy. It's a quiet, materially rich show for anyone drawn to painting that rewards close, slow looking.

shows.title: Familiars
shows.description:
Von Wolfe's paintings stage a menagerie of animals — crocodiles, night creatures, watchful predators — rendered in rich, glossy oil on canvas that gives even a small study the weight of a history painting. "Familiars" brings together new canvases ranging from an intimate 55 x 55 cm close-up to a large 180 x 180 cm centerpiece, "Night Visitor," suggesting a show built around scale as much as subject.

There's a storybook menace to the work: animals rendered with enough anatomical specificity to feel real, but staged and lit like symbols or omens rather than straightforward wildlife studies. For anyone who likes their painting a little uncanny, this is a tightly focused, visually punchy show.

shows.title: White Fence, Los Cholos
shows.description:
In 1986, on assignment for the documentary project "A Day in the Life of America," the great Mexican photographer Graciela Iturbide spent a day in a Boyle Heights household connected to the White Fence gang, one of East LA's oldest and most storied. What began as a brief assignment turned into an ongoing relationship that Iturbide returned to over more than three decades; this exhibition presents the photographs from that first 1986 visit, many never widely exhibited.

The pictures are notable for what they don't do: rather than sensationalizing gang life, Iturbide's black-and-white images register tenderness, domesticity and communal bonds, complicated by the fact that many of her subjects, including Rosario, Liza and Cristina, were Deaf as a result of the mid-1960s rubella epidemic and communicated through sign language — hand gestures that can look like coded signs but are, in fact, ordinary conversation.

Iturbide is one of the most significant documentary photographers of the past half-century. This show is a chance to see a tightly focused, historically rich body of work that treats a stigmatized Los Angeles community with unusual patience and respect.

shows.title: What's Goin' On
shows.description:
Greg Miller has spent more than three decades mining the visual debris of American popular culture — advertisements, comic panels, magazine clippings, movie stills, signage — and reassembling it into densely collaged paintings that read like scrambled transmissions from the postwar id. What's Goin' On is his latest body of work in that vein, combining photorealist passages with gestural abstraction and cut-and-pasted found material so that faces, logos, and fragments of text keep surfacing and receding within the same canvas.

The work sits at the intersection of nostalgia and unease: the imagery Miller pulls from is glamorous and familiar, but he distresses and interrupts it enough that the comfort curdles into something closer to cultural archaeology. It's less about a single narrative than about the accumulation of half-legible signals — the same overload of mediated memory that gave the 1960s and '70s their look, filtered through a contemporary hand.

Miller has particular history with this gallery: he was William Turner Gallery's first artist when it opened its doors in Venice in 1991, and this show marks another chapter in a relationship now well into its fourth decade. A longtime Venice resident who now splits time between Los Angeles and Austin, his paintings sit in the collections of LACMA, the Laguna Art Museum, the Crocker Art Museum and the Weisman Foundation, among others — a track record that gives this new work the weight of a career-long project still very much in motion rather than a victory lap.

shows.title: Hothouse
shows.description:
Randy Wray's new paintings continue his long engagement with organic, almost bodily abstraction — biomorphic forms rendered in thick, tactile oil paint that suggest flowers, cells, and swollen fruit all at once. His large canvas "Flower," worked over two years, gives a sense of the buildup and revision typical of his process: layers of paint accumulate like sediment until the image feels grown rather than composed.

Wray has spent decades working at the boundary between sculpture and painting, and that sculptural sensibility shows even in two dimensions — his forms have real weight and volume, pressing against the edges of the canvas. "Hothouse" suggests both greenhouse cultivation and fevered intensity, an apt frame for paintings that feel simultaneously nurtured and combustible.

shows.title: Felipe Suzuki
shows.description:
This untitled solo presentation brings Brazilian painter Felipe Suzuki's small, densely worked panels to Karma's Los Angeles space. Working in oil on canvas mounted on wood at an intimate scale, Suzuki builds still lifes and interior scenes that hover between representation and abstraction, with a compressed, almost jewel-like density of color and mark.

Suzuki has shown primarily in South America to date, and this marks a notable West Coast outing for an artist whose small-format paintings reward close, patient viewing rather than the sweeping glance a bigger canvas invites.

shows.title: The Shape of What Remains
shows.description:
Katherine Flynn is a Los Angeles-based photographer known for chasing forgotten places — motels with the vacancy sign still glowing, boats abandoned mid-lagoon, cars bleached by desert sun. This solo show at bG Gallery, her latest with the space after past exhibitions there, gathers new photographic work built around the same sensibility: color-saturated, slightly surreal scenes that read as documentary but feel staged by time itself.

Flynn has previously shown work that reframed found objects, including a series of photographs set into salvaged Volkswagen car doors, and that instinct for repurposing the discarded runs through this body of work too. Her images of empty swimming pools, roadside motels, and stranded vehicles turn the residue of American car culture and desert leisure into quiet, painterly compositions — evidence of past use now standing still.

The title, "The Shape of What Remains," points to what unites the pictures: an interest in the outline something leaves behind after its original purpose has drained away. It's an approachable but melancholic show, well suited to a gallery known for artists who work at the border of documentary and staged imagination.

shows.title: Spiritus Animales
shows.description:
Lara Kempke (also known professionally as Lara Eve Kempke) paints animals as if they were emissaries from another register of experience — birds, big cats and other creatures rendered in layered, richly textured mixed media that leans toward the mystical rather than the naturalistic. A Southern California artist with a background in fashion design, she brings a maximalist, pattern-driven sensibility to her canvases, building up surfaces with paint, collage and gilding until the animal subjects feel iconic, almost devotional.

"Spiritus Animales" (spirit animals) gathers this body of work at bG Gallery's Bergamot Station space. Expect vividly colored, densely worked compositions where a peacock, raven or big cat becomes a kind of totem — a stand-in for instinct, intuition, and the parts of ourselves we don't fully control. Kempke has described her practice as deeply intertwined with process and impulse, and that improvisational energy comes through in surfaces that reward close, slow looking.

Kempke's paintings are unapologetically decorative, emotionally direct, and easy to enjoy without a lot of art-historical throat-clearing.

shows.title: HAGS (Have a Great Summer)
shows.dates_note: Gallery's exhibitions page displays this group show (including a second hang, "HAGS II") as current with no exhibition dates published; local press reported it "opened in July" 2026 and remains on view with no closing date given.
shows.description:
HAGS — gallery-speak for "Have a Great Summer" — is Bruce Lurie Gallery's rotating summer group exhibition, bringing together the roster of emerging to mid-career artists the gallery has built its reputation on: painters, photographers, sculptors and mixed-media artists working across pop art, street art and abstract minimalism. It's a survey-style hang rather than a single-thesis show, meant to give a broad look at who the gallery represents.

This is the gallery's first extended summer show since relocating to its current Santa Monica Boulevard space after the January 2025 Palisades fire destroyed its previous location of five years. The larger, higher-ceilinged space gives the gallery more room to show sculpture and larger-scale paintings side by side, and owner Bruce Lurie — a veteran dealer whose career traces back to 1980s New York, including a stint assisting Leo Castelli — has used the show to reintroduce the gallery to its still-loyal Palisades collector base.

Because it's a group show without a single curatorial thread, visitors should expect variety: bold pop-inflected imagery, street-art-adjacent mixed media, and photography sitting alongside more painterly abstraction. It functions less as a statement show and more as a snapshot of where the gallery's program stands as it works to reestablish itself.

shows.title: Fragile Eternity
shows.dates_note: Gallery's exhibitions page displays this show as current (image uploaded August 2026); no opening or closing dates are published on the venue's own site.
shows.description:
Larisa Safaryan works in an unlikely material: eggshell. Born in Yerevan, Armenia and now based in Los Angeles, she hand-carves and stacks eggshell forms into sculptural and relief works that turn one of the most fragile substances imaginable into a meditation on strength, renewal and impermanence. "Fragile Eternity" at Bruce Lurie Gallery gathers this body of work, pairing the delicacy of the medium with a surprisingly durable, load-bearing physical presence.

Safaryan is self-taught, having come to art after two master's degrees in psychology and public management, and her lack of formal art training shows up as genuine invention rather than deference to convention — she treats the egg's curved surface as a canvas for ideas about rebirth and the passage of time. The results read alternately as devotional objects and as still lifes, each piece balancing precariousness against permanence.

For a gallery that has spent the last year rebuilding after losing its Pacific Palisades space to fire, a show built around fragility and resilience carries an obvious resonance. It's a quieter, more intimate counterpoint to the gallery's bigger group exhibitions, worth a visit for the sheer technical strangeness of the material alone.

shows.title: Live · Nude · Girls
shows.dates_note: Gallery's own homepage presents this as its current exhibition ("...is one of our most popular shows!") but publishes no opening or closing dates.
shows.description:
"Live Nude Girls" is Tracy Park Gallery's recurring flagship group show, a curated survey of nude photography, painting and sculpture that the Malibu Colony Plaza gallery describes as one of its most popular exhibitions. Rather than a single artistic statement, it's a wide-ranging look at how contemporary artists on the West Coast approach the nude figure — from straightforward figurative photography to more painterly and sculptural interpretations of the body.

The show draws on a roster of over a dozen artists working in different mediums, including photographers Vic Huber, Jamie Nelson and Matt Seidel, painters Reisha Perlmutter and Steve Shaw, and sculptor P.K. Comstock, among others. That range gives the exhibition an anthology feel: some works lean toward classical figure study, others toward more stylized or conceptual treatments of nudity and the body.

Tracy Park Gallery has operated in Malibu since 2004, building a program around supporting emerging and mid-career artists alongside a broader roster of West Coast talent, and this show is emblematic of that mixed, crowd-pleasing approach — accessible, visually direct work aimed at Malibu's gallery-going foot traffic rather than a tightly curated thesis show.

shows.title: Promised Lands: California's Unratified Treaties and Native Resilience
shows.description:
In the 1850s, federal commissioners negotiated eighteen treaties with California tribal nations promising reservation lands in exchange for ceding territory — treaties the U.S. Senate then quietly refused to ratify, leaving those promises legally void while the land was already gone. This traveling exhibition, developed with the National Museum of the American Indian and the Smithsonian Institution Traveling Exhibition Service, uses archival documents, protest ephemera, and contemporary Native-made objects to walk through that history and its long aftermath.

Objects on view include things like a spray-painted "Honor the Treaties" protest sign from 2017 and a coiled horsehair basket by Chumash artist Linda Aguilar that incorporates beads, shells, and even scavenged bingo markers and credit-card fragments — a piece that folds present-day material culture into a traditional basketry form. That mix of hard historical documentation and living contemporary art practice is the show's throughline: California's unratified treaties aren't a closed legal footnote, they're a condition Native communities in the state are still working within and responding to.

It's a smaller, more issue-driven show than the Autry's big collection surveys, built around a specific and under-told piece of California history. Worth planning around its late-September opening in the Samuel & Minna Grodin Gallery.

venue.name: Autry Museum of the American West

shows.title: A Human Pace: Robert Doisneau
shows.description:
Robert Doisneau spent more than five decades photographing Paris at street level, and this survey pulls together a wide swath of that career — lovers stealing kisses on rainy sidewalks, children turning gutters and stairwells into playgrounds, dogs waiting patiently outside cafés, and the ordinary tradespeople, musicians and strangers who populated his frame. It's the kind of material that made Doisneau one of the central figures of French humanist photography, working alongside contemporaries like Cartier-Bresson and Willy Ronis but with a gentler, more whimsical eye.

The checklist ranges from the 1930s through the 1970s and includes several portraits of fellow artists — Picasso with Françoise Gilot, filmmaker Jacques Tati — alongside the anonymous Parisians who make up the bulk of his archive. Doisneau worked mostly in gelatin silver, and the prints on view include both vintage and later prints pulled from his estate, giving a sense of how his negatives have continued to be revisited since his death in 1994.

What holds the show together is Doisneau's insistence that the street itself was the best director: chance encounters, caught at the right moment, outperform anything staged. For visitors who know him only from the famous kiss photographs, this is a chance to see how consistent and generous that vision was across an entire career, and why his pictures of postwar Paris remain some of the most beloved images in twentieth-century photography.

shows.title: In These Times: Recent Acquisitions at MOCA
shows.description:
MOCA takes stock of five years of collecting with this survey of recent purchases and gifts, organized not chronologically but thematically — rooms devoted to depictions of Los Angeles, group portraiture, new directions in abstract painting, and work obsessed with minute detail. It's the kind of show that functions as a status report on a museum's priorities: what MOCA's curators and donors have decided matters enough to acquire right now.

The roster spans generations and media, from painters like Louise Bonnet, Jacqueline Humphries, and Rebecca Morris to photographers Philip-Lorca diCorcia and Sawako Goda, sculptors Liz Larner and Diane Simpson, and artists working at the intersection of painting and social history like Andrea Bowers, Henry Taylor, and Vincent Valdez. Grouping the works by theme rather than by artist or date lets the show make quieter arguments about what recurs across a collection built by many different hands and donors over time.

For visitors who know MOCA's permanent holdings, this is a chance to see what's been added to the story since the last big collection rehang — and for those still working out what MOCA collects and why, it's as good an introduction as any to the museum's current curatorial thinking.

shows.title: Regime: Dramatis Personae
shows.description:
Alexander Apóstol's black-and-white portrait series casts LGBTQ+ activists in Caracas as stock characters from the theater of authoritarian power — the Dictator, the Masked Police Officer, the Ideological Tourist, the Propped-Up Paramilitarist — each posed with the studied body language of a political archetype rather than named as an individual. Shot in 2017 during a period of intense government repression in Venezuela, the ninety-image series draws on the artist's research into how gesture and posture get performed under populist and authoritarian rule, from independence-era heroes through the rise and fall of the Bolivarian Revolution.

Apóstol, a Venezuelan artist based in Madrid, frequently invokes the geometric abstraction of countrymen Carlos Cruz-Diez and Jesús Rafael Soto to needle at how national identity gets constructed and mythologized. By stripping his sitters of names in favor of social functions, he turns the portraits into a kind of civic taxonomy — a cast list for a political drama that keeps restaging itself. MOCA's presentation arrives as especially pointed given recent events in Venezuela, extending the work's original bite into an ongoing crisis.

This is a tightly focused, single-series exhibition rather than a full retrospective, well suited to close, patient looking at how photography can function as political theater criticism.

shows.title: To Hell and Back
shows.description:
New York-based artist Margaret MacLean makes her Los Angeles solo debut at induction gallery with this show, which the gallery describes as opening a new chapter for the space following Severin Hallauer's inaugural-season exhibition. Details on the work itself are sparse ahead of the opening, but the single released image — a close, textured view of a painted surface — suggests a practice grounded in material and mark-making rather than pure image-making.

Induction is a small project space tucked into a Westlake apartment building, the kind of low-overhead room where an artist's first LA showing can feel appropriately intimate rather than overproduced. Worth a visit for anyone tracking which emerging painters are getting their first foothold on the West Coast.

shows.title: Chapter 3: Interiors and Exteriors
shows.description:
The third installment in an ongoing series, Shanna Waddell's exhibition continues her project of building out an interior and exterior visual world in paint, moving between domestic scenes and the landscapes that frame them. As with the earlier chapters, the work reads as a kind of extended narrative told through discrete paintings rather than a single set of unrelated canvases.

Details on the specific works are still emerging as the show approaches its September opening, but Waddell's practice has consistently centered figuration grounded in everyday spaces — rooms, thresholds, the view through a window — treated with a painter's attention to how interior life and the built environment shape each other.

shows.title: Talk to Me
shows.description:
Vanessa Prager returns to Diane Rosenstein Gallery for her third solo show, an exhibition of new paintings that continues her long study of the human face pushed toward abstraction. Prager builds her portraits and figures out of thick, sculptural impasto, working the paint with palette knives until skin, hair, and background dissolve into ridges of pure pigment — you read the image at a distance and feel the material up close.

The Los Angeles-based artist has spent the past decade refining this push-pull between representation and mark-making, often returning to intimate subjects — lovers, friends, herself — rendered at a scale that makes the paint handling as much the subject as the sitter. Titles like "Affectionately" point to the emotional register she's after: warm, tactile, a little vulnerable.

For a gallery goer, this is a chance to see how far Prager has pushed her signature technique since her last outing here, and to catch a working method — thick paint laid on with tools rather than brushes — that photographs badly and rewards being seen in person.

shows.title: Charles Arnoldi
shows.dates_note: Venue's exhibitions page lists this as an "Upcoming Exhibition" with only "Opening Reception October 2" given; no closing date published yet.
shows.description:
Michael Kohn Gallery opens its fall season with a show devoted to Charles Arnoldi, the Los Angeles painter and sculptor who first made his name in the early 1970s fusing raw tree branches into wall-relief constructions before turning that same physical, material-forward sensibility toward vibrantly colored abstract paintings.

Arnoldi came up alongside the Light and Space and Finish Fetish generations in LA but took a rougher, more improvisational path — his work has always been about direct construction rather than illusion, whether he's laying branches into a panel or building up layered, jigsaw-like fields of color on canvas. Now in his eighth decade of practice, with pieces in the permanent collections of MoMA, the Whitney, and the Art Institute of Chicago, he remains one of the defining figures of postwar Los Angeles abstraction.

Details on the exhibition's full scope weren't yet published at the time of writing, but the gallery's announcement image — a close-up of dense, gestural color — suggests a survey of his recent, energetically worked paintings. Worth checking back on for confirmed dates and checklist as the opening approaches.

shows.title: Textile Alchemy: The Art of Reiko Sudō and NUNO
shows.description:
For more than forty years Reiko Sudō has run NUNO, a Japanese textile collective that treats fabric-making as a kind of alchemy — fusing traditional handicraft with industrial technology and unlikely materials to produce cloth that architects and designers around the world have sought out. This is billed as the largest retrospective of her work to date, with more than a hundred limited-edition textiles shown alongside the drawings, sketches, tools, and prototypes that reveal how each piece actually gets made.

What comes through is Sudō's collaborative process: she works constantly with independent artisans and regional workshops across Japan, and the exhibition frames her practice as much about preserving disappearing craft traditions as about producing beautiful objects. For anyone who thinks of textiles as a secondary art form, this show makes the case that Sudō's inventive material experiments belong in the same conversation as painting or sculpture.

venue.name: Los Angeles County Museum of Art (LACMA)

shows.title: Home of the Future, 1925–1985: Designing Domestic Utopias
shows.description:
Between 1925 and 1985, American designers and manufacturers kept promising that a better life was one gadget away — self-cleaning kitchens, plastic houses that could be assembled in a day, push-button appliances, and eventually the desktop computer. This exhibition gathers the architectural models, drawings, films, and consumer objects — everything from kitchen sinks to television sets — that sold those visions of domestic utopia to the American public.

What's most interesting is the exhibition's stated interest in who got left out of these futures and who imagined alternatives to them; a show about mid-century optimism that also asks pointed questions about whose home was actually being designed for whom. It's a great pick for anyone into design history, postwar consumer culture, or the strange gap between advertised futures and lived reality.

venue.name: Los Angeles County Museum of Art (LACMA)

shows.title: The Kitchen and Its Discontents
shows.description:
Two landmark kitchens from LACMA's design collection anchor this compact show: Margarete Schütte-Lihotzky's efficiency-driven 1926–30 "Frankfurt Kitchen," designed for German social housing, and Charlotte Perriand and Le Corbusier's 1948–50 kitchen for the Marseille Unité d'Habitation. Both were engineered around modernist ideals of order and labor-saving design, built explicitly with women's domestic work in mind.

Photographs, prints, and advertisements from the collection complicate that tidy modernist narrative, showing the mess, friction, and unpaid labor that these "rational" kitchens didn't actually eliminate. Presented alongside the concurrent Home of the Future, it's a sharp, feminist-inflected footnote to that larger survey — proof that the history of domestic design is also a history of whose comfort was being engineered, and at what cost to whom.

venue.name: Los Angeles County Museum of Art (LACMA)

shows.title: The Brockman Gallery: Los Angeles, 1967–1990
shows.description:
Founded in South LA by brothers Alonzo and Dale Brockman Davis in the wake of the Watts Rebellion, the Brockman Gallery became one of the most important incubators for Black artists in Los Angeles for over two decades — a space that gave early support and exhibitions to David Hammons, Suzanne Jackson, Carrie Mae Weems, and many others before their careers took off. This is billed as the first large-scale museum exhibition dedicated to that history, and it treats the gallery itself as a work of art: a community-built institution as significant as anything shown inside it.

With more than sixty artworks across media plus archival material — photographs, ephemera, correspondence — the show reconstructs both the visual output the Davis brothers championed and the social infrastructure they built around it. It's an essential corrective for anyone whose picture of 1970s and '80s LA art history skips over the galleries and spaces that operated outside the traditional (and traditionally white) commercial circuit.

venue.name: Los Angeles County Museum of Art (LACMA)

shows.title: You'll Find Yourself
shows.description:
Raymond Argumedo works in small, glowing panel paintings that fuse cosmic imagery with figures rendered like devotional icons — halos of stars, mystic flora, and celestial light standing in for interior states. His pieces feel closer to relics than illustrations, mixing pop-surrealist polish with a genuinely spiritual undertow.

"You'll Find Yourself" gathers new acrylic-on-panel works that continue Argumedo's ongoing series of cosmic portraits, where figures dissolve into or emerge from swirling galaxies and botanical patterning. The paintings are compact and jewel-like, meant to be studied up close, and the show continues Thinkspace's longstanding support of the artist within its New Contemporary program.

Expect a tightly hung solo presentation in the gallery's West Adams space, with an opening reception on September 12 giving visitors a chance to meet the artist directly.

shows.title: Dark Energy
shows.description:
"Dark Energy" is a solo turn for the artist KCN, whose title points toward the invisible forces that shape and pull at things — a fitting theme for work that operates in the New Contemporary vein Thinkspace has championed since 2005, where surreal imagery and pop-cultural iconography stand in for psychological and cosmic undercurrents.

Details on the specific body of work are still emerging as the show opens, but the gallery has slotted it into its September lineup alongside solo presentations from Raymond Argumedo and Alex Achaval, suggesting a run of dream-logic, figure-based painting across the space.

Visitors can catch the artist in person at the September 12 opening reception, part of a full night of new exhibitions across the gallery's West Adams space.

shows.title: A Place To Live
shows.description:
Alex Achaval paints quiet, moody oil interiors and landscapes where light does most of the emotional work — a lamp-lit room, a hazy field, a figure caught in the moment just before or after something happens. His palette leans toward dusk tones, and his compositions favor stillness over spectacle, closer to painterly memory than narrative illustration.

"A Place To Live" gathers new framed oil-on-canvas works that continue this sensibility, with titles like "Unspoken," "Weather Eye," and "Collective Notion" hinting at the show's interest in the emotional weather of domestic and interior space — the idea of "place" as psychological as much as physical.

The show opens alongside several other September solo presentations at Thinkspace, with a shared opening reception on September 12 giving visitors a chance to see Achaval's newest paintings in person.

shows.title: Spotlight on Local Creatives (with Ella-V-Ella | Juliette Toma | Daisy Murray)
shows.description:
Session Seventeen brings together three artists — Ella-V-Ella, Juliette Toma, and Daisy Murray — for a group presentation of new work.

As with prior Fresh installments, the show functions as a snapshot of the current local scene rather than a single unified theme, letting each artist's individual approach stand on its own within a shared gallery space.

It opens September 12 with a joint reception alongside the gallery's other new September exhibitions, making for a full night of openings at the West Adams space.

shows.title: Visual and Verbal Cognition
shows.description:
Theodore Svenningsen has spent decades working across two parallel bodies of work, and this solo show at Wonzimer puts them side by side. One strand is textual: paintings and works on paper that use plain, everyday language — about money, belonging, mortality, and the isolation of not fitting in — as both content and formal material, letting words sit as flat, declarative objects on the surface. The other is the "Structures" work, spanning series like the Primitive Structures and Anxious Objects, murky black-and-white compositions of half-recognizable forms glimpsed behind grids and architectural scaffolding, closer to apparition than illustration.

Svenningsen's background is unusual for a painter: he trained in philosophy at UCLA to the doctoral level before finishing an MFA in painting at Otis, and that history shows in the show's operating premise — that verbal and visual cognition are two distinct, only partially overlapping ways of knowing, and that putting both types of work in one room lets each throw the other's limits into relief. It's a quiet, cerebral exhibition, more interested in doubt and ambiguity than resolution, from an artist who has had pieces enter MoMA's collection while remaining a relatively under-the-radar figure in Los Angeles.

shows.title: Jack Whitten: The Numinous
shows.description:
Following his acclaimed 2025 retrospective at MoMA, Jack Whitten gets a focused historical show at Hauser & Wirth's Downtown LA flour-mill campus, honing in on paintings and works on paper from the 1980s — a decade that began with a studio fire and ended with some of the artist's most technically audacious breakthroughs. This is deep-catalog Whitten rather than greatest-hits: the Soulspace paintings and circular acrylic reliefs that gesture toward celestial navigation, pixel-like grids that anticipate his later tesserae technique, and Site paintings cast directly from manhole covers and tire treads.

Whitten spent his career pulling abstraction away from gesture and toward material invention — peeling, casting, and layering paint until it behaved more like sculpture than pigment. This show catches him mid-transformation, fusing formal experimentation with the spiritual and political charge that runs through his work on Black identity and animist belief. It's a rewarding show for anyone who thinks they already know postwar American abstraction; Whitten's 1980s output complicates that story in the best way.

The exhibition opens September 30 alongside Glenn Ligon's concurrent show at the same location, making for a strong single visit to the gallery's reopened downtown campus.

shows.title: Views of Pagan, Burma, 1976-78
