shows.description:
German photographer Ursula Schulz-Dornburg has spent decades documenting landscape and architecture at the edges of political and historical memory, and this show returns to some of her earliest sustained work: black-and-white photographs made in Pagan (Bagan), Burma between 1976 and 1978. The ancient temple field, one of the world's great concentrations of Buddhist monuments, becomes in her hands less a tourist monument than a study in erosion, silence, and scale.

These Pagan pictures — made decades before her better-known Cold War and Middle East bodies of work — show the same patient attention to structures left to time and weather. It's a quiet show, built for looking slowly.

shows.title: Lights Form Action!
shows.description:
Ashoke Chhabra brings a body of sculptural lamp and light work to ace/121's project space in this solo show, built around illuminated forms that read as much as small-scale sculpture as they do functional objects. The gallery's own preview material centers on a detailed octopus-form lamp base, suggesting an exhibition rooted in playful, biomorphic silhouettes rendered in glowing, tactile materials.

Chhabra's practice sits at the intersection of craft object and gallery sculpture, and this show continues ace/121's pattern of championing Glendale-based and regional artists working in unconventional materials. Expect a tightly installed single room hung and lit to let each piece's glow do double duty as both artwork and ambient installation lighting.

Given the gallery's intimate scale, this is a good show for viewers interested in lighting design, ceramics, and assemblage as much as traditional painting or sculpture — a reminder that the ace/121 artist colony continues to support offbeat, materials-driven practice in the shadow of the YMCA parking structure.

shows.title: You and I
shows.description:
Kwame Brathwaite (1938–2023) was the photographer behind the "Black Is Beautiful" movement of the 1960s, documenting Harlem's jazz clubs, the Grandassa Models, and the cultural politics of natural hair and Black self-image alongside his brother's African Jazz-Art Society and Studios collective. This exhibition, co-curated by actor and activist Jesse Williams with the artist's son Kwame S. Brathwaite (director of the Kwame Brathwaite Archive), pulls together vintage and later prints spanning self-portraiture, fashion, and street photography.

The works on view move between the intimate and the iconic: a self-portrait of Brathwaite with his Argus C3 camera sits alongside images of models like Sikolo in ruffled dress, a jazz quartet caught mid-performance, and children on a Harlem swing set. Together they trace how Brathwaite's camera doubled as an instrument of cultural advocacy — turning fashion and portrait photography into a visual argument for Black pride well before the phrase became a slogan.

Having represented the Brathwaite archive for several years, Philip Martin Gallery continues to give this pivotal but still under-recognized photographer serious gallery treatment in Los Angeles, pairing rarely seen prints with the historical framing that Williams and Brathwaite's son bring as co-curators.

shows.title: 40 Year Anniversary Exhibition
shows.dates_note: Page presents this as two consecutive shows: "Part One: Oct 2nd – Nov 1st" and "Part Two: Nov 6th – Nov 29th," saved here as one continuous run through Nov 29.
shows.description:
La Luz de Jesus marks four decades in business with a two-part anniversary exhibition, split into back-to-back installments each with its own opening reception.

Given the milestone, expect the anniversary show to function as something of a highlight reel — likely drawing on the gallery's deep artist roster and past exhibition history rather than presenting a single new body of work. The two-part structure (with a changeover and second opening in early November) suggests a rotating cast of contributors across the eight-week run.

For longtime followers of the lowbrow and pop-surrealist scenes, this is a rare chance to see the gallery reflect on its own history in real time, with two separate opening nights to catch different configurations of the show.
shows.reception: Friday, October 2 and Friday, November 6, 7-11pm each night

shows.title: Gathering
shows.description:
Zoe Walsh takes over ICA LA's 7th Street facade with a commissioned, site-specific mural — the museum's outdoor project slot for the fall season. Walsh, a Los Angeles painter with an MFA from Yale, builds their compositions through digital modeling, hand-cut stencils, and screen printing, layering photographs of queer community and chosen family staged in their own garden with material drawn from queer archives and topographic maps.

The resulting images read as silhouetted bodies suspended in gardens, parks, and urban landscapes — scenes that treat the city's green spaces as sites of queer intimacy reclaimed from erasure. Rather than a single fixed image, Walsh's process of superimposition and refraction keeps the picture plane unstable, so figures shimmer in and out of legibility depending on where you stand and how the light falls on the facade.

This mural extends ideas Walsh has explored in solo shows at Vielmetter and Yossi Milo, translating a studio practice built on canvas into a public-facing, weather-exposed format that will live on the building through the winter. It's a free, walk-by way to encounter an artist whose gallery work usually requires stepping inside.

venue.name: Institute of Contemporary Art, Los Angeles (ICA LA)

shows.title: Our Strange Hollows
shows.description:
Amia Yokoyama's first institutional solo show fills ICA LA's Project Room with ceramic sculpture, holography, painting, and experimental animation — a body of work that treats metamorphosis as both subject and method. Yokoyama, who trained in experimental animation at CalArts and attended Skowhegan, moves clay and light through repeated cycles of breakdown and repair, letting each material's instability stand in for the porousness of bodies and identities under pressure.

The show's title points to an interest in negative space and the underworld: hollow forms in bronze and glass become portals rather than absences, mining ancient mythologies of descent and transformation. Yokoyama has described her ceramics practice as a "dialog with earth, fire, water, and air" that carries political and ritual histories inside ordinary-seeming objects, and that same logic extends to her holographic pieces, where a fragment is built to contain the whole.

It's a compact but ambitious presentation from an artist who has shown at the Armory Center for the Arts and Jeffrey Deitch, and a good entry point for anyone curious about how sculpture and moving image can be made to behave like liquid.

venue.name: Institute of Contemporary Art, Los Angeles (ICA LA)

shows.title: Grounding Bodies, Casting Dreams
shows.description:
This is less a conventional exhibition than a live community ritual staged inside ICA LA: a collaboration between the museum's Agency of Assets youth fellowship and Hwa Records, a collective of Korean diasporic artists and healers-in-residence at the museum. Together, teenage fellows and the resident artists are building a Dol Top (돌탑), a stone tower rooted in Korean geomancy traditions meant to spiritually protect a village — here reimagined as a protective gesture for the fellowship's young participants.

Visitors are invited to participate directly, bringing a stone from home or the surrounding landscape to the front desk to add to the accumulating tower; at the close of the show, the rocks are ceremonially returned to the local Tongva/Los Angeles landscape rather than kept as artifacts. It's a project about displacement, care, and communal repair, growing out of Hwa Records' work processing the effects of anti-Asian violence and generational trauma through gathering and craft.

Worth seeing as much for the process as the object — the tower will look different depending on when you visit, and the show doubles as a showcase for the mentorship and paid-employment model that Agency of Assets runs with Downtown and East LA high schoolers.

venue.name: Institute of Contemporary Art, Los Angeles (ICA LA)

shows.title: Bite The Hand That Feeds You
shows.description:
Phung Huynh's third solo show at Luis De Jesus centers on an unlikely charged object: the pink donut box that has become an emblem of Cambodian refugee entrepreneurship in Southern California. Huynh, a Cambodian-Vietnamese refugee artist based in LA, draws directly onto and around these boxes in graphite, building documentary-style drawings, paintings, and sculptural installations that hold both the sweetness of the family business mythology and the exhausting, racialized labor underneath it.

The work pointedly rejects the "grateful refugee" narrative baked into American resettlement rhetoric. By reclaiming the idiom "bite the hand that feeds you" — usually deployed to silence complaint — Huynh reframes who is actually doing the feeding: immigrant and refugee labor sustaining industries that then target those same communities through immigration enforcement. It's a body of work that uses something as mundane as a donut box to talk about debt, gratitude, and who gets to tell the story of arrival.

Huynh's work sits in LACMA's and the Pacific Asia Museum's collections, and this show continues her long-running interest in using intimate, everyday materials to unpack the costs of displacement and assimilation.

shows.title: Inheritance
shows.description:
June Edmonds extends her well-known Flag series with new paintings that treat the American flag as an unstable, contested symbol rather than a fixed monument. Working in a deep, deliberately expanded palette of browns, Edmonds interrupts her "Standing Flag" compositions with abstract stains — blights, scars, phantom topographies — that read as unresolved history pushing up through the stripes.

A newer, more intimate strand of the show, the "Draped Flag" works, releases the canvas from its rectangular support entirely; cinched at the center, these loose, child-sized forms evoke hoodies and children's clothing, a direct address to the adultification and endangerment of Black youth, from Emmett Till to Tamir Rice and Trayvon Martin. It's a shift from monument to garment, from symbol to body.

Edmonds, an LA-based painter who had a mid-career survey at LMU's Laband Art Gallery in 2021 and holds a Guggenheim Fellowship, continues to use color theory — specifically the range and dignity of brown — as both formal strategy and political argument. This is her fourth show with the gallery and a clear escalation of the ideas she's been building for years.

shows.title: Idea of North
shows.description:
Ben Tong's second solo show at Night Gallery is built around the idea that a painting shouldn't sit still. Working in oil, Tong pushes pigment across the canvas with brushes, rags, and — distinctively — a massage gun, producing radial, semi-controlled bursts of color that behave like light passing through stained glass or wind moving through a landscape. Moons, rainbow arcs, and starlike flares recur across the work, giving the paintings a charged, almost transmitting quality.

The title borrows from Glenn Gould's 1967 radio documentary of the same name, and Tong is explicit about thinking in terms of frequency and signal — light as something that can be received rather than just depicted. It's a body of work shaped by the particular quality of Southern California sun, treating each canvas as if it were already lit from within before a single brushstroke.

Tong, an LA-based painter who previously showed The Violet Hour at the gallery, works in a mode that resists fixed concepts in favor of intuitive, doubt-tolerant process — action generating meaning rather than the reverse. Worth seeing for anyone interested in painting that treats color and surface as an active, moving field rather than a settled image.

shows.title: The Blab! Show
shows.dates_note: Venue's future-exhibitions page says only "COMING SEPTEMBER 12," no closing date published; this is Copro's long-running annual Blab! Show group exhibition curated by Monte Beauchamp.
shows.description:
Every September for over two decades, Copro Gallery has handed its walls over to Monte Beauchamp, the founder and longtime editor of the underground graphics-and-comics annual Blab!, for a sprawling group show pulling together the illustrators, painters, and printmakers who've populated the magazine's pages. Past editions have drawn seventy-plus contributing artists at a time, mixing lowbrow and pop-surrealist veterans with newer names working in painting, sculpture, and illustration.

Given the gallery's track record, expect a dense, maximalist hang: darkly funny, technically virtuosic work that sits at the crossroads of fine art and outsider comics culture, the kind of show that rewards slow looking piece by piece. The gallery hasn't yet published this year's full checklist or an official title beyond "coming September 12," but based on two decades of precedent this is effectively the newest edition of the Blab! Show, one of Bergamot Station's most anticipated recurring events.

Copro's two exhibition spaces in the back corner of Bergamot Station have long been ground zero for LA's pop-surrealist and dark-illustration scene, and this annual show remains one of the best single snapshots of that world working today.

shows.title: Joseph + Melinda Ostraff
shows.description:
Nüart Gallery's Santa Monica outpost pairs husband-and-wife artists Joseph and Melinda Ostraff for a two-person show of new work. Joseph Ostraff, a longtime Brigham Young University professor and three-time Utah Arts Council fellowship recipient, makes richly patterned, densely layered paintings that read as a kind of personal cartography — abstracted shapes and architectural motifs that track how people convert raw space into meaningful place. Melinda Ostraff, who holds a PhD in environmental science and human geography, brings a research-driven eye to her own practice, and the pairing sets his painterly abstraction against her more systematic investigations of landscape and place.

Joseph Ostraff was born in Santa Monica, giving this Bergamot Station presentation a homecoming undertone, and his gradated, patterned canvases — with titles referencing places from Berlin to the Lofoten Islands — suggest an artist still mapping his own relationship to geography decades into a well-traveled career.

This is a compact, one-month run, timed for Nüart's fall Santa Monica program, and offers a chance to see two connected but distinct sensibilities in dialogue in the gallery's Bergamot Station space.

shows.title: Wayne Thiebaud
shows.dates_note: Venue's exhibitions page lists this show only as "Fall 2026," with no specific opening or closing dates published.
shows.description:
Leslie Sacks Gallery devotes its fall program, alongside "Focus Female," to a concentrated selection of prints by Wayne Thiebaud, the Sacramento painter best known for his creamy, confectionary still lifes of cakes, pies, and diner counters. This presentation focuses on his graphic work: lithographs from the 1994 portfolio "The Physiology of Taste" — images of desserts, bistro sketches, and cafe scenes rendered with Thiebaud's signature thick, sugary color and long cast shadows — alongside an etching from his 1979 "Recent Etchings II" series.

Thiebaud's prints translate the same appetite for everyday American subject matter that made his paintings famous into the more intimate, linear language of lithography and etching. The rooster, sorbet, and dessert-tray subjects on view here carry the same deadpan affection for ordinary abundance that has made his work instantly recognizable for over half a century.

It's a modest, connoisseurial show rather than a blockbuster, well suited to Leslie Sacks' longstanding specialty in modern and postwar works on paper, and a good opportunity to see Thiebaud's printmaking practice up close rather than through reproductions of his more famous paintings.

shows.title: Amadeo Luciano Lorenzato
shows.description:
Lorenzato (1900–1995) is one of the great outsider figures of Brazilian modernism: a house painter and itinerant laborer from Minas Gerais who didn't take up easel painting seriously until his sixties, after decades spent working in Brazil and briefly in Italy. This presentation, David Zwirner's fourth show devoted to the artist and his first ever in Los Angeles, gathers small-scale paintings of the everyday scenes around his hometown of Belo Horizonte — hillside houses, kitchen tables, potted plants, church façades — rendered in flattened, almost geometric blocks of saturated color.

What makes Lorenzato's paintings compelling is the tension between their modest subject matter and their sophisticated formal intelligence: thick, deliberately built-up surfaces (he often used a palette knife to lay paint on like plaster) turn ordinary domestic views into something closer to abstraction. There's a kinship with self-taught painters like Bonnard's more naive cousins, but also a direct line to the color logic of Brazilian concretism, despite Lorenzato never being formally part of that movement.

For Los Angeles audiences this is a rare chance to see a substantial body of work by an artist far better known in Brazil than in the U.S., and one whose reputation has grown steadily since his rediscovery late in life. Expect landscapes, interiors, and still lifes that reward close, slow looking.

shows.title: Manzanita
shows.description:
Daniel Gibson's third solo show with the gallery is built around eleven modestly scaled oil pastel paintings on linen, hung close together along the wall so they read almost like pages of a single unfolding book. The works move between the observed and the invented — desert rock formations, wildflower fields, granite morteros once used by the Kumeyaay to grind seeds — filtered through a loose, automatic drawing process that lets forms surface intuitively rather than by plan.

The title refers to a plot of land Gibson owns near the Mexican border in San Diego County, and to one of the Kumeyaay tribal bands whose history is woven into the imagery of stone and desert. Recurring throughout is the painter's palette itself, appearing as landscape feature, held aloft like a talisman, or merged with a figure's head — a symbol, in Gibson's words, of painting as a means of getting through uncertainty.

Gibson, who lives and works in Los Angeles, has spent the last several years developing a distinctive visual vocabulary around the California and Baja desert — a mix of folk-art flatness, hallucinatory color, and personal mythology. With his recent transition into fatherhood surfacing as a quiet undercurrent (a desert dove named for his daughter recurs in several works), Manzanita reads as a meditation on inheritance, memory, and the desert as a site where deep time and personal history overlap.

shows.title: Silke Otto-Knapp
shows.description:
Presented in Regen Projects' viewing rooms alongside Elliott Hundley's main-gallery exhibition, this focused selection of small paintings and studies revisits the singular watercolor-on-canvas technique of Silke Otto-Knapp (1970–2022), the German-born, Los Angeles-based painter and longtime UCLA professor who died in 2022. Many of the works are being shown publicly for the first time.

Otto-Knapp built her paintings through a process of controlled erasure: layers of black watercolor applied to canvas, sprayed with water, then scrubbed and scraped away to let the white primer beneath emerge as figure and light. The results hover between representation and abstraction — grayscale dancers, stage sets, and landscapes that draw on her wide-ranging enthusiasms, from Bronislava Nijinska's choreography to Georgia O'Keeffe, Ingmar Bergman, and the coastal light of Fogo Island.

Because several works on view are preparatory studies for larger, later paintings, the exhibition doubles as a window into Otto-Knapp's process — how an intimate, exploratory mark could scale up into the monumental multi-panel works for which she's best known. For anyone who has encountered her paintings in museum collections from LACMA to MoMA and Tate, this is a rare chance to see the workings behind them.

shows.title: Keith Sonnier: Inside Light, 1968–1970
shows.description:
This is a focused historical survey of the earliest, most experimental years of Keith Sonnier's career, honing in on 1968 to 1970, when the Louisiana-born artist first began bending neon and argon gas into sculpture. Sonnier, who died in 2020, is remembered as one of the great postwar American sculptors, and this show captures the moment he found his signature material: glowing tube light paired with the raw fixtures, transformers, and wiring that power it. Works like the two-tone "Arced Neon" pieces from 1968 show him testing single gestures in colored light, while the later, more elaborate "Neon Wrapping Incandescent V" (1970) shows a fast-maturing vocabulary of layered, multicolor form.

What makes this body of work compelling beyond its historical importance is how physical it still feels — these are sculptures that depend on their walls and corners the way a painting depends on its stretcher bars, casting shadow and colored light into the room and implicating the viewer's own silhouette in the composition. Sonnier arrived at these ideas while still a student, in dialogue with contemporaries like Eva Hesse and Bruce Nauman, and this exhibition makes the case for how radical that dialogue with industrial materials and immaterial light really was.

It's a tightly scoped, jewel-box kind of show rather than a full retrospective, but for anyone interested in postminimalism, the history of light as sculptural material, or just wanting to see real neon glow in person, it's worth the visit.

shows.title: Pierre Leguillon: Ads & Brands
shows.description:
Pierre Leguillon is less a traditional artist than a career-long collector and re-arranger, and this two-part presentation across the Marciano's Window Gallery and Library makes his archival instincts the whole show. In "Ads," he draws from decades of advertisements in which artists — Marina Abramović, Andy Warhol, Joseph Beuys, Salvador Dalí, among many others — appear as models or brand ambassadors, an ongoing collection of over 250 images that's been curated here specifically for Los Angeles. Seeing artists sell McDonald's, Dior, and liquor next to each other says a lot about how celebrity and cultural capital operate outside the gallery walls.

The second half, "Brands," transplants a piece of Leguillon's own Brussels institution The Museum of Mistakes into the MAF Library — a sprawling, non-hierarchical accumulation of ephemera, printed matter, and oddities (a painted pair of Doc Martens shows up alongside a sock collection) that treats the museum itself as a kind of book, and the book as a museum. It's a strange, funny, research-driven show about how images and objects circulate and gain meaning through display and repetition rather than through any single masterpiece.

Leguillon has shown at the Louvre, WIELS, and the ICA Boston, and his cataloguing sensibility rewards patient, close looking rather than a quick walkthrough — budget real time if advertising, art-world mythology, or archival art practice interests you.

shows.title: Jon Ching (new work)
shows.description:
Jon Ching paints hyperrealist, symbolically loaded scenes that fuse the human figure with plant and animal life — skin sprouting ferns, hands cradling anemones, faces dissolving into coral and fungus. It's a style that sits at the intersection of natural history illustration and surrealism, built on meticulous oil-painting technique and a recurring interest in ecological fragility and interconnectedness.

This new exhibition at KP Projects (also known as Merry Karnowsky Gallery) continues that body of work; based on the gallery's past presentations of Ching's paintings, expect densely detailed, jewel-toned compositions of hybrid creatures and human/nature mergers, rendered with a naturalist's precision. Ching has built a substantial following for this niche of botanical-surrealist realism, and past shows here have sold out quickly, so the opening reception is the moment to see the work in person before it disperses into private collections.

shows.title: Last time I met you the world was a different place
shows.description:
Joakim Ojanen returns to Richard Heller Gallery with a new body of glazed stoneware sculptures, paintings, and works on paper populated by his signature cast of soft, lumpy, big-eyed figures. The Swedish artist, who trained in ceramics almost by accident after abandoning an illustration degree in Stockholm, has spent the last decade building a visual vocabulary that reads like a comic strip crossed with a folk-art shrine — hunched boys, sad dogs, and blobby creatures rendered with a craftsman's touch for glaze and surface.

This is Ojanen's latest solo outing with the gallery that has shown his work in Los Angeles since his 2016 debut, and the title alone hints at the wistful, slightly melancholic humor that runs through his practice: figures that seem to be quietly working through loneliness, awkwardness, and the strangeness of getting older, even as the forms themselves stay playful and inviting. Fans of his earlier shows here, like "A Show for the Lonely Distant Baby Souls" and "Year of the Dog," will recognize the emotional register even as the specific characters and glazes are new.

Worth seeing for anyone drawn to the intersection of ceramics and cartooning — Ojanen's work sits comfortably alongside artists like Ryan Travis Christian and Eric Croes, also on Heller's roster, who share an interest in turning offbeat, intimate feeling into tactile, handmade objects.

shows.title: Museum-in-Residence at Hama
shows.dates_note: Venue page says the exhibition is "Beginning June 15th, 2026" and describes it as "an exhibition project that unfolds over the next three months," with no exact closing date published.
shows.description:
For its Museum-in-Residence project, Venice Heritage Museum has taken its archive out of its own building and installed it inside Hama Sushi, the Windward Avenue restaurant that has anchored that stretch of Venice since 1979. The presentation builds on portraits and ephemera already displayed at the restaurant, adding new material — a sweeping 1913 panorama of the Venice lagoon shot from roughly the same vantage as the traffic circle where Hama now sits, a contemporary aerial photograph by Venice-based artist Hso Hkam that mirrors that historic view, and reproduction ephemera like a 1939 Venice Mardi Gras matchbook.

The show is paired with excerpts from VHM's oral history project, including interviews with Hama's own owner Esther Chaing, longtime surfboard shaper Guy Okazaki, and other longtime residents — turning a casual dinner spot into an informal annex of the museum's collection.

It's a low-key but genuinely site-specific idea: using a business that has itself become part of Venice's history as a vehicle for looking at the neighborhood's disappearing landmarks and community memory. Worth a look for anyone eating at Hama over the summer, though visiting hours are the restaurant's own dinner hours rather than the museum's weekend hours.

shows.title: Textiles as Monument
shows.artist: Suchitra Mattai, Jagdeep Raina, and Swapnaa Tamhane
shows.dates_note: Venue page says "Now Open" with no published closing date; opening celebration event was held Aug 8, 2026.
shows.description:
Three artists of South Asian descent — Suchitra Mattai, Jagdeep Raina, and Swapnaa Tamhane — use textile as a way of building memorials to people history has left out of its monuments. The Fowler commissioned new work from each artist, made in dialogue with the communities the pieces honor, turning cloth, thread, and weave into what the museum's own framing calls counter-monuments: forms that claim public memory without bronze or stone.

The result is an exhibition that plays against expectation — where a monument is usually rigid, permanent, and singular, these works are soft, layered, and collaborative. Expect large-scale hangings, dyed and braided fiber installations, and pieces that draw directly on South Asian craft traditions like weaving, embroidery, and quilting, reworked into contemporary sculptural forms that fill the gallery volume rather than sitting flat on a wall.

It's a strong pairing with the Fowler's broader interest in objects, migration, and whose stories get preserved — worth seeing alongside the museum's other current shows on Ifugao rice culture and the afterlives of African art objects, all of which circle similar questions about memory, possession, and who gets to be remembered.

shows.title: Julie Shafer | Jennifer Celio
shows.description:
as-is pairs two Southern California artists who both work at the boundary between document and invention. Julie Shafer is a photographer and educator whose practice examines the human imprint on landscape — she's made large-format work photographing industrially damaged terrain, and has spoken of her images as a way of walking through the ghosts a place leaves behind. Jennifer Celio, by contrast, works mostly in drawing and mixed media, mining the visual clutter of the built environment — vintage typefaces, mid-century design, personal ephemera — into dense, precise compositions that ask you to look slowly.

Both artists share a history with the loose Los Angeles network of artist-run spaces (Celio was a longtime member of Durden and Ray), and this isn't the first time their work has crossed paths at as-is — Shafer previously appeared there in a three-artist show built around politically engaged, lens-based practice. Pairing her photographic record of place with Celio's drawn accumulation of urban detail sets up a productive friction between the documentary and the invented.

as-is has built its reputation over more than a decade as one of downtown's steadiest small exhibition spaces, consistently giving veteran and mid-career Los Angeles artists tightly focused, single- or double-artist shows rather than sprawling group surveys — this one continues that pattern.

venue.name: as-is.la
hours: By appointment; check site for open hours during exhibitions

shows.title: Open Sesame
shows.description:
Alexa Guariglia paints tightly composed interiors and figure studies in gouache, watercolor, and ink on paper, a combination that gives her scenes an odd, matte flatness even as the imagery leans theatrical and cinematic. Chairs, drapery, and figures caught mid-gesture recur across her compositions, staged with the lighting and framing of a stopped film still — a sensibility that fits a show titled Open Sesame, with its implication of a door swinging open onto some private, slightly heightened world.

Guariglia builds her larger paper works — some reaching five or six feet across — the way a painter might build a canvas, layering washes and opaque gouache passages until the paper takes on real weight and shadow, quite a feat on a support usually reserved for something lighter and more immediate. That tension between the modesty of the material and the ambition of the scale is a big part of what makes her work distinctive.

This is a two-person hang at Moskowitz Bayse, paired with Franziska Goes's Seeds and Circles in the gallery's adjoining space — worth the trip to see both bodies of work in dialogue, one rooted in figuration and narrative, the other in geometric abstraction.

shows.title: Seeds and Circles
shows.description:
Franziska Goes makes hard-edge abstractions built from grids, dots, and repeated geometric units — paintings that read at first like exercises in systematic color logic before you notice how much she lets the system wobble. A grid tilts, a color runs slightly warmer than its neighbor should allow, sand and modeling paste rough up an otherwise smooth acrylic surface. It's abstraction with an engineer's structure and a painter's appetite for friction.

The German-born, LA-based artist's canvases in this show span from crisp, brightly colored grid paintings to newer, more textured works that incorporate sand and paste into the acrylic, giving the surface a tactile, almost topographic quality that photographs can't quite capture — worth seeing in person for that reason alone.

Seeds and Circles hangs alongside Alexa Guariglia's Open Sesame at Moskowitz Bayse, setting Goes's cool geometric vocabulary against Guariglia's theatrical figuration — two very different ways of using structure to organize a picture.

shows.title: discrepancies with E.S. (in company): The Neutra VDL House
shows.description:
Leonor Antunes turns the Neutra VDL House itself into her material, threading a suite of new sculptures through Richard Neutra's glass-walled studio and residence. Rather than simply installing objects in the space, she measures and re-derives forms from the furniture and architecture of Elizabeth Scheu Close, a Viennese-Jewish émigré architect who moved in the same circles as Neutra but was turned away from his office decades ago. The result is a quiet historical correction disguised as abstract sculpture: hanging cedar forms strung from stainless steel poles in the upstairs living room, curved acrylic-and-brass screens echoing a childproofing gesture Close made in her own house, and a leather floor piece patterned after her brick pathways.

Antunes has spent years building a body of work out of the overlooked designs of modernist women — this show also folds in earlier pieces referencing Cuban designer Clara Porset and French designer Charlotte Perriand. Seeing the work installed inside an actual mid-century house, rather than a white-box gallery, gives the project unusual stakes: viewers can compare Antunes's abstracted "measurements" directly against the real staircases, sun louvers and pocket gardens that inspired them.

Given Antunes's exhibition history — Venice Biennale representation, and surveys at SFMOMA, the New Consequence Museum, and Kunsthalle Basel — this is a rare chance to see her work in Los Angeles, and specifically in dialogue with the city's own architectural history.

shows.title: subterranean convergence
shows.dates_note: Clockshop's site confirms an opening reception and performance on Saturday, October 24, 2026 at LA State Historic Park; no closing date is published for the installation itself.
shows.description:
Commissioned by Clockshop, LaRissa Rogers's subterranean convergence turns a stretch of LA State Historic Park — once the site of the Southern Pacific River Station — into a fragmented, simulated railroad. Chinoiserie-style tracks cast in tabby (a lime-and-shell concrete) carry reproductions of more than fifty objects contributed by community members and institutions across Los Angeles and New Orleans, each chosen for its personal or historical weight. The piece traces the old "Sunset Limited" line that once connected those two cities, using the train as a metaphor for the migrations — forced, hopeful, and everything in between — that shaped both places during Reconstruction and the Great Migration.

Rogers, a sculptor and University of Virginia professor whose work has shown at Documenta 15 and the Wattis Institute, built the project around a score for live performance, developed with collaborator Michelle Sui, that activates the installation on opening day. Because the work sits outdoors on public parkland rather than behind a gallery door, it's as much a piece of civic infrastructure as it is sculpture — visitors can walk the tracks and handle the archive of cast objects long after the opening weekend's performance has ended.

venue.name: Clockshop at Los Angeles State Historic Park

shows.title: Stalking the Wild Pendulum
shows.description:
Ramiro Hernandez paints in a soft-focus, technicolor haze that reads at once as nostalgic and unsettling — sun-bleached beach scenes hang beside images of weaponry and police equipment, all rendered in the same hazy, Richter-adjacent glow. The Oakland-based painter takes his exhibition's title from Itzhak Bentov's 1977 book on consciousness and holograms, using the idea that "every ripple can mechanically be traced back to the source" as a loose organizing metaphor for a body of work that moves between violence and calm without much visual distinction between the two.

It's a show about how images flatten difference: an idyllic day at the beach and a piece of military hardware can occupy the same fuzzy, sentimental register once they're run through Hernandez's palette. He's showing recently at galleries like Massey Klein and Harkawik in New York and BOZOMAG in LA — this is his first solo outing at Dominique Porter.

shows.title: Chris Lux
shows.description:
Los Angeles painter and ceramicist Chris Lux returns to GGLA for a solo turn after a run of collaborative and group appearances at the gallery, including 2024's Revel Hall installed inside a derelict Mt. Washington house. Lux works in a flattened, ultra-bright register — often using Flashe vinyl paint — that borrows the graphic punch of stained glass and early-20th-century woodblock prints while staying rooted in a distinctly Southern Californian strain of outsider-adjacent figuration.

His recurring cast of frog-people, saints, and domestic still lifes reads like folklore rewritten for a skate shop: cooperation, adoration, and low-grade menace all play out in flat, saturated color fields outlined in confident black line. Lux extends the same sensibility into glazed ceramic lamps and objects, treating functional forms with the same cartoon-mythic seriousness as his paintings.

Given his history of installing work in unconventional settings, expect this show at GGLA's Glassell Park space to lean into both the paintings and the sculptural lamp works that have become a signature of his practice.

shows.title: California Visionaries: The Lives and Legacies of Walt Disney and Hubert Eaton
shows.description:
Walt Disney and Forest Lawn founder Hubert Eaton might seem like an odd pairing for an exhibition, but the two men — both transplants from Missouri who built California institutions steeped in fantasy, showmanship, and death-adjacent spectacle — were genuinely close, with Disney serving as an honorary pallbearer at Eaton's funeral before dying himself a few months later. This show, timed to the 60th anniversary of both men's deaths, traces that friendship through Disneyland attraction concept art, sheet music from the Disney Music Legacy Library, and previously unseen photographs pulled from the Forest Lawn archive.

It's a strange, specific bit of California history — two men who each turned death, memory, and myth-making into a business, and who apparently recognized something of themselves in each other. For families who already associate Forest Lawn with its famous stained glass and Great Mausoleum murals, this is a lighter, more pop-cultural entry point into the museum's collection.

shows.title: 75 Years: Art Finds a Home at Forest Lawn
shows.dates_note: Venue page gives only "Opening September 19, 2026" for this exhibition; no closing date is published.
shows.description:
Marking 75 years since the Hall of Crucifixion-Resurrection opened in 1951 (with the Forest Lawn Museum following in 1952), this archival exhibition digs into the institution's own history rather than showing outside artists. Expect never-before-exhibited photographs from the museum's archive, remastered audio from the original Hall of the Crucifixion program, and artworks that haven't been on view in nearly a decade — plus attention to overlooked figures, like first museum director Mary Hunt, who built the place from what started as a memento shop.

For a museum best known for its enormous history paintings and stained glass, this is a chance to see the institutional backstory instead — how a cemetery's gift shop grew into a sculpture collection and, eventually, a public art museum with free admission.

shows.title: Dye Trace
shows.artist: Abby Flanagan, Hai-Wen Lin, and Marina Darcy Weiner
shows.description:
Dye Trace brings together three artists — Abby Flanagan, Hai-Wen Lin, and Marina Darcy Weiner — for a group exhibition at IZZY LEE, the Chinatown gallery formerly known as North Loop West. The gallery has spent the past several years cultivating a roster that moves fluidly between Los Angeles and the Northeast (it grew out of a project space in Williamstown, Massachusetts), and this show continues that cross-country conversation with new work from each artist.

While the gallery has not yet published a checklist, the title points to processes of saturation, staining, and residue — the kind of slow chemical or material transformation that recurs across a lot of the painters and object-makers this space has shown before, from Beverly Acha's mineral-toned abstractions to Andrew Holmquist's layered geometries. Expect an exhibition built around close looking at surface and process rather than a single unifying subject.

Dye Trace opens after the gallery's usual August closure, marking its first show back on Chung King Road for the fall season. It's worth a stop both for the work itself and as a chance to see how the gallery's identity is settling under its new name.

shows.title: Come When Mi Call Yu
shows.description:
Lenworth McIntosh's first solo exhibition with OCHI imagines a Black commune in a lush rural valley, bracing for a storm that reads as both weather and spiritual reckoning. Working from his childhood memories of Jamaica and the visual grammar of animation, McIntosh renders ghostly ancestral presences moving alongside the living: a man ladling soup for the group, elderly women singing in a circle of light, figures dissolving into cloud and color.

The paintings draw specifically on the Caribbean "Nine Nights" wake tradition, in which mourners gather for nine nights of food, music and storytelling to send a loved one's spirit onward. McIntosh translates that communal, celebratory mourning into an earthy, saturated palette and loose, cartoon-inflected figuration that keeps the work feeling alive rather than elegiac.

McIntosh, who lives and works in Los Angeles, follows up a 2025 solo presentation at Frieze Los Angeles with this debut gallery show. It's a good entry point for viewers curious about how diasporic memory and folklore get reworked through a very contemporary, animation-adjacent painting language.

shows.title: She who sits
shows.description:
Adrienne Elise Tarver's paintings center on Vera Otis, a fictional matriarch the artist built over a decade of work after finding an unnamed woman's photo in a secondhand shop. Otis is styled after mid-century Black screen icons like Dorothy Dandridge and Eartha Kitt, but instead of performing for the camera, she simply sits — resting, watching, taking up space without asking permission. That stillness is the whole argument of the show: rest as agency, not passivity.

These particular paintings began as a much larger public project — a Public Art Fund commission that put Otis's image on some 300 bus shelters and newsstands across New York, Boston and Chicago in 2024. Seeing the paintings themselves, rather than the billboard versions, lets you sit with the layered source material Tarver works from: family snapshots, found photographs, and clippings from vintage Ebony and Jet magazines collaged into an invented but historically textured biography.

Tarver, who teaches at Pratt and lives in Brooklyn, has shown at institutions including the Aldrich Museum and Atlanta Contemporary; this is her latest outing with OCHI, which represents her.

shows.title: Sangam
shows.description:
Raghav Babbar spent time at the 2025 Maha Kumbh, the Hindu pilgrimage that drew what's been described as the largest religious gathering ever recorded, and this show is his attempt to paint his way through that scale. Rather than a single hero or holy figure, Babbar's canvases dissolve individual pilgrims into a churning, nocturnal crowd — bodies caught mid-gesture between exhaustion, ecstasy and prayer, rendered in a muted, earthen palette that owes an evident debt to European history painting.

That's a deliberate move on Babbar's part: he's spoken of wanting to bridge Goya-style crowd painting with the specific, documentary reality of a contemporary Indian pilgrimage. It's a shift for an artist who built his early reputation on intimate portraiture — here the crowd itself becomes the subject, with darkness functioning less as absence than as a shared, primal space.

This is Babbar's first US solo exhibition, staged simultaneously with a booth at New York's Armory Show. Born in Rohtak, India and now based in London, Babbar has had a fast rise — a 2025 Arts Council England Global Talent Visa, a spot on Forbes' 30 Under 30 Asia list, and works already in the permanent collections of ICA Miami and the Kiran Nadar Museum of Art. Worth seeing for anyone interested in how a young painter handles mass spectacle without losing the individual.

shows.title: Rough Ways of The Delicate Ones
shows.description:
Emmanuel Louisnord Desir works across painting, assemblage and sculpture to dig into colonialism, spirituality and the long shadow of biblical narrative — particularly the Abrahamic traditions and how they echo across diasporic history. The works on view (with titles like "Fury of the Saints," "Hellenization of Jacob," and "SOS Radio Telescope") suggest an artist reaching for cosmic and scriptural language to talk about displacement and inherited belief.

Desir's assemblage pieces incorporate found and industrial materials — engine parts, radio components — alongside more traditional painted surfaces, giving the biblical references a scavenged, present-tense grounding rather than treating them as historical illustration. The effect is less devotional than interrogative: sacred stories reframed through the wreckage of contemporary material culture.

This is a Los Angeles solo outing for the gallery's program, running alongside a concurrent Herman Cherry exhibition at Sebastian Gladstone's New York space — a reminder of how this young transatlantic gallery is building out its roster on both coasts.

shows.title: Black Florals
shows.description:
Henri Paul Broyard's second solo show with Tyler Park Presents is built around a single, deceptively narrow idea: painting flowers and houseplants entirely in black. Broyard has circled floral still life throughout his career but always avoided the genre's cozy, domestic connotations; rendering the plants in black strips out the sentimentality and turns them into graphic, almost architectural silhouettes that hover between the viewer and a richly colored ground.

The paintings build outward from total abstraction — blocks of color, stripes, grids — before Broyard lets figuration emerge, and he'll sometimes paint back over a resolved image to return it to abstraction, leaving traces of the erased picture underneath. Alongside the paintings, the show continues his series of repaired terracotta and Bauer pots, mended with construction adhesive and metal brackets in a blunt, American riff on kintsugi — vessels that stay visibly broken even as they're made whole again.

Broyard, a Los Angeles native trained at CCA and in Peter Doig's class at Düsseldorf's Kunstakademie, has shown at 12.26 in Dallas, Post Gallery in Zurich and Foreland in the Catskills; his work sits in the collections of the Portland Museum of Art and the California African American Museum.

shows.title: Ovum
shows.description:
Roxanne Jackson's ceramic menagerie of hybrid, half-fossilized creatures lands at The Pit for what the gallery describes as her first solo presentation in her home state of California. The new sculptures grew out of a residency at Cal State Long Beach's Center for Contemporary Ceramics, and the ambition of that time in the studio shows: large-scale creatures share the room with smaller, more intimate objects, all circling around the idea of the egg as an origin point for wild, unstable life.

Jackson treats clay less as a medium than as living tissue — glazes and lusters read like scale, bark, or bone, and every piece keeps visible traces of the kiln's unpredictability rather than smoothing them away. A serpent wraps around a vessel, a bird's body splits open, a harpy hoards silver treasure in her nest; the show works a rich seam of natural history and myth without settling into either.

It's a good showcase for an artist whose work sits at the noisy end of the current wave of figurative ceramics — funnier, grosser, and more unruly than most, with a real command of glaze as a tool for storytelling rather than decoration.

shows.title: Life on Earth
shows.description:
Chase Biado's new paintings mark a shift away from the invented fantasy worlds of his earlier work toward scenes drawn from ordinary life — a figure reading the newspaper, a drive through smoke-hazed air, a walk through an orchard — rendered with just enough distance to feel like half-remembered dreams rather than documentary. Desaturated color and loose, atmospheric brushwork do a lot of the talking; a single stroke stands in for rain, a smear for a passing car, so the paintings read as much as records of weather and motion as they do as pictures of people.

Showing alongside Roxanne Jackson's ceramics in The Pit's Atwater Village space, Biado's quieter, more melancholic paintings offer a contrast in temperature and material while sharing an interest in transformation and impermanence.

shows.title: Idols In Bloom
shows.description:
Rafael Megall's paintings work a rich, jewel-toned register somewhere between religious icon and botanical still life, with figures and floral motifs rendered in the flattened, gilded planes of devotional art. Idols In Bloom leans into that vocabulary directly, pairing the language of veneration with the fragility and excess of flowers in full bloom — worship and decay held in the same frame.

This show looks to be a good showcase for Megall's particular fusion of the sacred and the decorative, ornate surfaces built up with the patience of an icon painter but aimed at very contemporary anxieties about beauty and impermanence.

shows.title: REALMS
shows.dates_note: Venue page says the exhibition is "opening Friday, September 4 at 7 PM - 10 PM"; no closing date is published yet.
shows.description:
Devin Flynn has spent decades in the margins between disciplines — as an animation director behind the web series Y'all So Stupid, as the bassist in the band Pixeltan, and as a longtime collaborator of underground comics figure Gary Panter. REALMS is his most defined gallery presentation yet, pulling together years of drawing, collage, and mixed-media work into a survey that traces how his visual language has developed alongside his music and animation careers rather than separately from them.

The show's centerpiece is a new series called OTOFORMS, which folds a literal sound element into the work — a fitting move for an artist whose visual and musical practices have always been intertwined. MutMuz is supplementing the new pieces with a survey of earlier works on paper, posters, prints, and drawings upstairs, plus a program of animation screenings running throughout the exhibition, so visitors get both the new focused body of work and the decades of drawing that led up to it.

Flynn's LA roots run deep: he came up in the city's 1980s graffiti scene under the tag RELM before moving into animation and music, and the show's title nods to that history as much as to the idea of his output existing across separate creative "realms." It's a fitting subject for MutMuz.

shows.title: Lollipop
shows.description:
Adam Higgins has spent the last several years painting salads — specifically, bird's-eye views of Caesar salads loaded with sardines, raw shrimp, croutons, and improbable amounts of dressing, rendered with the obsessive, all-over density of a Pollock drip painting crossed with a 17th-century Dutch still life. Lollipop, his new show at Chris Sharp Gallery, continues that project while widening its frame: recent bodies of work have folded in photographic fragments underneath the food — a Parisian street, a yacht-dotted seascape, the artist's own truck — so that the salad becomes a kind of screen or portal onto other pictures and other places.

Higgins, who earned his MFA at Yale and lives and works in Los Angeles, treats the salad-as-subject as a deadpan device: funny on its face, but built with real formal seriousness around composition, palette, and the history of still life painting. The joke never undercuts the craft — dense layering of paint, tondo and rectangular formats borrowed from culinary photography, and a persistent tension between abstraction and legible imagery.

This is Higgins's latest solo outing with the gallery that has represented him since his breakout "My Salad Years" series, a body of work that has since traveled to Paris and been featured at fairs including Independent. Expect a tightly hung gallery of oils on linen and canvas that reward close looking — the closer you get, the more the salad dissolves into pure paint.

shows.title: Collective Noise
shows.dates_note: Venue's own site lists Jun 12–Aug 21, 2026 for this exhibition page, but the homepage still marks it "ON VIEW NOW" with "EXTENDED!" as of early Sept 2026 and gives no new closing date, so end_date is left open pending a later pass.
shows.description:
Krikor Tchay is a self-taught Armenian-American painter working in mixed media — acrylic and spray paint built up in dense, layered passages that read somewhere between graffiti, abstract expressionism and pop collage. Collective Noise gathers a body of his recent canvases that circle around vulnerability, desire and resilience, using clashing color and gestural mark-making to visualize emotional static: the "noise" of competing feelings that most people carry quietly.

The paintings on view lean into contrast — hard graphic edges next to loose drips, saturated color fields interrupted by scratched-in text and figures — a language Tchay has been refining since his 2018 "Tangled" series. It's unpretentious, autobiographical work made by an artist who has built his following largely through Instagram and word of mouth rather than gallery representation, which makes this extended run at Eye For Sound (a small storefront space run in partnership with a neighborhood coffee shop) a good chance to see a substantial group of his paintings together in person rather than as scattered studio posts.

shows.title: Chris Lux
shows.description:
Chris Lux is a San Francisco-based painter and collagist known for densely layered canvases that stack figure drawing, comic-book imagery, sculptural elements and even painted architectural fragments into single compositions — sometimes expanding into full painted rooms that swallow the viewer along with the artwork. He has been showing steadily since 2008, including an earlier immersive installation, Absinthe, that turned an entire gallery room into one continuous painted environment.

This solo show at GGLA (Guerrero Gallery's Los Angeles outpost in Glassell Park) brings his layered, referential style to the gallery's Verdugo Road storefront. Expect the same interest in "portals to the past" that defines his practice: images and tiles of imagery — drawn from history, literature and pop culture — arranged so the eye is constantly renegotiating what it's looking at, a painting inside a painting inside a studio.

Lux's exhibition continues that program with an artist whose work rewards slow, close looking rather than a quick glance.

shows.title: Mangia! The Evolution of Italian Food in the United States
shows.dates_note: IAMLA's site lists this as an open, current exhibition (linked under "Upcoming Exhibitions" but confirmed live via press coverage as of summer 2026); the museum's own pages publish no exact opening or closing date, though outside press reports it running "through summer 2027." Saved with dates left open pending a later confirmation pass.
shows.description:
Mangia! traces how Italian immigrants reshaped what America eats, using the tools of a history museum rather than an art gallery: vintage advertising, restaurant ephemera, photographs, and everyday objects pulled from nearly a century of Italian American food culture. The show is organized thematically, opening with the poverty and hardship that drove waves of immigration between 1876 and 1914 before following those immigrants' recipes and enterprise into the mainstream of American life.

What makes the exhibition compelling is its attention to specific, often overlooked through-lines: the Americanization of dishes like fettuccine alfredo and spaghetti and meatballs, the rise of espresso culture, and the surprising Italian American roots behind household names like Planters Peanuts and Tropicana. A wall of restaurant t-shirts, hats, and other memorabilia gathered from close to 100 eateries nationwide gives the show a scrapbook intimacy, while a large national map lets visitors flag historic Italian restaurants of their own.

Housed in the Italian Hall, a 1908 landmark building in the heart of the old Little Italy, IAMLA is a small but earnest museum, and this show plays to its strengths: it's not trying to be comprehensive art history, but a warm, well-researched piece of cultural storytelling about identity, migration, and the dinner table. It's an easy, free, and worthwhile stop for anyone curious about the immigrant history baked into American food culture.

venue.name: Italian American Museum of Los Angeles (IAMLA)

shows.title: Darren Cortez and Tanya Brodsky
shows.description:
This two-person exhibition pairs Darren Cortez, whose paintings often traffic in gothic, folkloric imagery — crows, blades, ritual objects rendered with a graphic, tattoo-flash intensity — with Tanya Brodsky, an LA sculptor who reworks found urban hardware (security bars, bed frames, rolling gates) into wry, body-conscious objects. Both artists share an interest in taking materials loaded with menace or utility and bending them toward something stranger: Cortez through image-making steeped in memento-mori symbolism, Brodsky through a sculptural practice that sandblasts and re-chromes the architecture of domestic security into objects that read as almost tender.

Brodsky, who was born in Kyiv and trained at RISD and UC San Diego, has spent years mining the visual language of window bars and fences — devices meant to keep bodies out or in — and turning them into sculptures that flirt with humor, vulnerability, and camp; her public commission "Yolki Palki" carried that same colorful, industrial-materials sensibility into a West Hollywood streetscape. Cortez's paintings, seen in NOON's recent group shows, favor a stark, illustrative style that draws on tattoo culture and outlaw iconography.

Pairing the two suggests a show interested in toughness as a surface that can be cut into, softened, or reclaimed. Expect a mix of wall-based painting and object-sculpture that plays off each other's hard materials and soft undertones.

shows.title: Remains of the Day
shows.description:
Michel Auder has spent more than sixty years pointing a camera at whatever was in front of him — friends, lovers, hotel rooms, television screens, the inside of his own apartment — and this show pulls together the photographic side of that restless archive. Auder was one of the first artists to treat portable video as a real medium rather than a novelty, and the black-and-white and color photographs here function less like discrete artworks than like frames pulled out of a much longer continuous take. Alongside the stills, moving-image works extend the same logic into time.

Auder's decades of documenting Warhol-era downtown New York (he crossed paths with Alice Neel, Cindy Sherman, Hannah Wilke, and Larry Rivers, among others) give the work a specific historical weight, but the images on view are presented as an open-ended visual archive rather than a greatest-hits survey — records of looking as much as records of who was in the room.

The exhibition is accompanied by a book of the same title, treated as an extension of the show rather than a catalogue afterthought, with tactile photographs on the wall placed in dialogue with the printed page. Opening day includes a 3pm conversation between Auder and curator Hamza Walker, followed by a reception.
shows.reception: Saturday, September 12, 5-7pm (artist talk with Hamza Walker at 3pm)

shows.title: Dye Trace
shows.artist: Abby Flanagan, Hai-Wen Lin, and Marina Darcy Weiner
shows.description:
Dye Trace brings together three artists whose work moves through textile, garment, and process-based logic. Abby Flanagan has shown with this gallery's Williamstown program previously (as "Earshot"), working in a mode that treats material handling — soaking, staining, layering — as its own kind of drawing. Hai-Wen Lin, a Taiwanese-American artist whose practice grew out of fashion and body-garment training at SAIC, builds sculptural and wearable forms — kites, textiles, and body-adjacent objects — that read as both craft object and conceptual gesture about extension and flight. Marina Darcy Weiner works in textile and ceramic-adjacent processes, with a recent output of pieced and dyed cloth pieces that share the show's evident interest in staining and trace as a working method.

Grouping these three suggests a show built around the literal and metaphorical residue of process: dye, stain, mark — evidence of a hand or a chemical reaction left behind on cloth or paper. It's the kind of small, tightly considered group show this gallery (recently rebranded from North Loop to IZZY LEE, though still operating out of the same Chung King Road storefront) tends to favor — three practices in conversation rather than a survey.

Worth a visit for anyone tracking textile-forward practices working the line between craft and conceptual art in Los Angeles right now.

shows.title: UAC: The Never Again Now — Child | Separation | Detention | Resistance
shows.dates_note: Venue's future-exhibitions page lists the show "Coming August 29, 2026" with an opening reception that date; no closing date is published anywhere on the site.
shows.description:
Oscar Magallanes turns the Museum of Social Justice's galleries over to the bureaucratic language of immigration enforcement, borrowing the federal designation "unaccompanied alien child" for a show that traces what that acronym does to real families from southern Mexico and Central America now living in the Westlake neighborhood a few blocks from the museum's Olvera Street home. Expect a mix of original artworks, installation elements, and archival material — the kind of assemblage-driven, documentary approach Magallanes has used elsewhere to connect present-day immigration policy to older histories of displacement and cultural erasure.

The show is less an art exhibition in the white-cube sense than a community history project with visual art as its anchor: it's paired with documentary screenings, workshops, and public discussions meant to extend the conversation past the gallery walls. That civic-minded, testimony-based approach fits squarely with the museum's mission of presenting Los Angeles history from the perspective of the poor, immigrants, and other marginalized groups.

Worth seeing for anyone interested in how contemporary artists are responding to immigration detention and family separation policy, and for the museum's rare willingness to let a single, sustained community project fill its whole exhibition program rather than mounting a survey show.

shows.title: Dancing in the Pocket
shows.description:
Gabriel Slavitt makes paintings and reliefs out of house paint, drywall mud, and wood filler — hardware-store materials pushed into the register of fine-art surface. Working in Los Angeles, he hand-carves wood panels to match the contours of his own sketchbook drawings, then stretches or wraps canvas over them and builds up the image mark by mark, often with improvised tools like chopsticks or sewing needles standing in for brushes. The result sits somewhere between painting, relief sculpture, and drawing — surfaces that read as loose, doodled gestures until you notice how laboriously they were constructed.

Dancing in the Pocket is Slavitt's newest body of work at Babst, following prior solo and group presentations at the gallery including What Is Wrapped in Heart Cloth and The Loss That Shapes the Image. His pieces have circulated through a mix of contexts — from academic project spaces to L.A. galleries like Vielmetter — and consistently return to the same questions: what a mark retains of the hand and material that made it, and how a domestic, unglamorous palette (house paint, drywall compound) can still carry real feeling.

Expect a continuation of Slavitt's carved-panel paintings alongside ink drawings on paper, the two bodies of work he tends to develop in tandem — sculptural pieces built slowly over weeks and spontaneous sumi or India ink drawings made in a single sitting. Worth a visit for anyone interested in artists who treat construction materials as a legitimate painting medium.

shows.title: Final Projects: Group LIX - spindrift LIX
shows.artist: Alexandra Kahl, Axel Koschier, and Sarah Silbernagel
shows.description:
Every six months, the MAK Center's Artists- and Architects-in-Residence program closes its cycle with a final-projects show at the Mackey Apartments, and this edition — Group LIX, titled spindrift LIX — presents new work by three residents: Sarah Silbernagel, an architect and filmmaker whose work engages social housing and participatory planning through film; Axel Koschier, an Austrian sculptor working across installation and mixed media; and Alexandra Kahl, whose practice spans posters, collage, flags, artist books, and video.

The show is necessarily a brief one — four days, capping a six-month residency — but it's a rare chance to see work made specifically in response to Rudolph Schindler's modernist Mackey Apartments, a building the residents have lived and worked in throughout their stay. Koschier arrives having recently shown at Art Sonje Center in Seoul; Silbernagel's films have been presented at the Venice Architecture Biennale and MUMOK Vienna.

Worth catching for anyone interested in the overlap between architecture and art practice, and in the MAK Center's role as one of the few L.A. institutions built around an international residency model rather than a permanent collection.

venue.name: MAK Center for Art and Architecture — Mackey Apartments
hours: By exhibition and event schedule; see makcenter.org

shows.title: Play Date: Toys by Artists
shows.description:
Curated by Axel Wilhite, this group show takes its cue from a landmark 1975 exhibition that asked artists to design toys rather than art objects, and runs with the idea across seven decades and seventy-odd contributors. Chris Burden's original Spyder-Man, made for that 1975 show, anchors the exhibition alongside newly commissioned toys by a wide swath of Los Angeles's sculptors, painters, and ceramicists — from veterans like Peter Shelton, Tony Berlant, and Gwynn Murrill to younger names working in wood, clay, and cast metal.

The premise is playful but not slight: toys are treated here as a serious testing ground for ideas about scale, function, and imaginative possibility, the same terrain sculpture occupies but with a built-in permission to be funny, tactile, and a little absurd. Expect a dense salon-style hang of small, handled objects rather than precious wall-bound pieces — something closer to a toy chest than a white cube.

Wilhite has also produced a limited-edition "five-suit" poker deck as an exhibition catalog, with each artist's toy represented as a card — a nice structural joke that doubles as a keepsake and a curatorial index of the show. Two artist talks during the run (September 19 and October 3) will bring some of the 69 participating artists into the gallery to discuss the work directly.

shows.title: As the Moonbird Flies
shows.artist: Shane Cotton, Simone Griffin, Fiona Pardington
shows.description:
1301PE brings together three New Zealand artists — Shane Cotton, Simone Griffin and Fiona Pardington — whose work, in different mediums, keeps returning to questions of land, ancestry and the natural world as seen through a distinctly Māori and Pacific lens. Cotton is known for layered, symbolically dense paintings that mix Māori motifs, birds and colonial-era imagery into unsettled historical landscapes; Pardington works primarily in photography, often turning her lens on natural history specimens and taonga (treasured objects) to meditate on loss, memory and colonial collecting practices.

The show's title nods to migration and flight — apt for a gallery pairing that gathers three distinct practices under one roof and asks them to speak to a shared set of concerns about place and passage. It's a rare chance for Los Angeles audiences to see contemporary New Zealand art in depth, since none of these three shows regularly on the West Coast.

Given 1301PE's history of championing under-recognized international artists (Uta Barth, Diana Thater and others got early support here), this show is worth catching both for the work itself and as a signal of where the gallery's attention is turning next.

shows.title: The Hour of the Pearl
shows.description:
Jonathan Ryan takes his exhibition's title from a line in Steinbeck's Cannery Row describing the hush of early morning before the sun rises — a threshold moment between night and day that becomes the show's governing mood. Ryan, a Buffalo-born, LA-based painter with an MFA from Tyler School of Art, has built a body of work around exactly these liminal states: light that hasn't decided what it is yet, figures caught in transitional interiors, the strange clarity that appears right before ordinary vision resumes.

Ryan's paintings tend to work in hazy, saturated color and soft-edged forms, giving even mundane domestic scenes an charged, almost hallucinatory quality. He has shown previously at the Landing in LA and Hesse Flatow in New York, and was recently included in a group show at the Utah Museum of Contemporary Art, signaling a painter whose quiet, atmospheric canvases are gaining wider institutional notice.

This is one of three concurrent solo presentations opening the same week at Megan Mulrooney's Santa Monica Boulevard space.

shows.title: The End of a Long Line
shows.description:
Omaha-based painter Falon Stutzman returns to Megan Mulrooney following her 2025 debut solo show there, Woman Having a Hard Time, which introduced her flattened, cartoon-inflected figures caught in states of quiet emotional overload — waiting tables, curled up with a dog, stalled mid-gesture. The End of a Long Line looks to continue that project of turning everyday female personhood into something both comic and faintly tragic.

Stutzman paints in oil and flashe, building scenes with bruised, queasy color and spatial distortions borrowed from animation and New Wave film stills. Her figures are archetypes rather than portraits — generic enough to be anyone, particular enough to sting. She's a Columbus College of Art and Design graduate whose work has appeared in New American Paintings, and this second LA solo suggests a gallery relationship still very much building momentum.

The show opens alongside two other solos at Megan Mulrooney.

shows.title: Conjuror
shows.description:
Tommy May's Conjuror is the third of three solo shows opening simultaneously at Megan Mulrooney this September, filling out the gallery's rotating three-room format. May works as a painter whose practice leans toward invented, theatrical imagery — the title itself points to sleight-of-hand, transformation, and the idea of pulling something unexpected out of ordinary materials.

Details on the specific works are still emerging as the show approaches its opening, but May's inclusion alongside Jonathan Ryan and Falon Stutzman continues Megan Mulrooney's pattern of pairing painters with distinct, often uncanny takes on figuration and atmosphere within a single exhibition cycle.

Visitors can expect to see all three shows in one visit to the gallery's Santa Monica Boulevard space, a format that has become a signature of how Megan Mulrooney programs its calendar since opening in 2024.

shows.title: Michael LeVell: Salient Forms
shows.description:
Michael LeVell has been drawing and painting architecture and interiors for nearly forty years, working out of Tierra del Sol's Claremont studio program since its founding in 1989. His signature medium is layered colored pencil and acrylic on paper, rendering rooms, facades, and furniture pulled loosely from the pages of design and architecture magazines. The forms come out geometric and saturated — flattened planes of color that snap into believable perspective even as they dissolve into pattern and texture built from repeated, obsessive mark-making. He extends the same vocabulary into clay, producing rough-hewn slab sculptures that read as three-dimensional companions to the works on paper.

Billed by the gallery as a survey of five decades of his output, this show pulls together drawings, paintings, and ceramic pieces spanning LeVell's career, tracing how his handling of interior space has shifted from tightly bordered architectural studies toward looser, more abstracted geometric fields. The recurring hand-drawn borders and frames that edge many of his pieces give the flat compositions an odd sculptural presence, as if each drawing were also a small building.

LeVell's work has traveled well beyond the gallery that represents him — group showings at Outsider Art Fair and Felix Art Fair, and past recognition from mainstream critics — and this exhibition is a rare chance to see the arc of his practice assembled in one room rather than in single-artist snapshots.

shows.title: Doyle Lane: Master of Clay
shows.description:
Doyle Lane spent decades in Los Angeles quietly redefining what a clay vessel could be, and this retrospective — the first devoted to him at a major museum — finally gives his career room to breathe. The show spans from his compact, glossy "weed pots," sold for years at studio-craft fairs and flea markets, to the room-sized tile murals he made on commission for Southern California architects like William Pereira and Welton Becket, several of which have rarely if ever left the buildings they were made for.

What comes through is Lane's obsession with glaze as a painter's material: surfaces mottled and pooled with color in ways that put him in conversation with the era's abstract painters as much as with fellow ceramicists like Peter Voulkos. The exhibition doesn't shy away from the harder context either — Lane worked for decades as a Black artist largely excluded from the gallery system that celebrated his white contemporaries, and much of this material is being publicly seen for the first time thanks to years of research with his family, friends, and collectors.

With more than a hundred objects on view, including the Huntington's own 18-foot Mutual Savings and Loan mural, this is as complete a picture of Lane's practice as has ever been assembled, and a chance to see a genuinely under-recognized California modernist get his due.

venue.name: The Huntington Library, Art Museum, and Botanical Gardens

shows.title: Laura Aguilar: Day of the Dead
shows.description:
This is the lesser-seen half of a two-part rotation devoted to Laura Aguilar, the San Gabriel Valley-raised Chicana photographer who spent her career photographing the body — often her own — with unusual candor. Where the museum's spring presentation focused on Aguilar's landscape self-portraits, this fall rotation turns to an earlier body of work: black-and-white photographs made between 1984 and 1992 documenting Día de los Muertos celebrations across Los Angeles.

Rather than staged portraiture, these images read as documentary work from inside a community — artists, couples, and families active in the city's Chicano art scene, photographed at altars and gatherings that Aguilar clearly had ongoing access to. It's an early, less-exhibited chapter of her career, and a useful complement to the more widely reproduced nude self-portraits that later made her name.

Drawn from recent acquisitions from Aguilar's estate, the show is part of the Huntington's expanded commitment to Aguilar's work following her death in 2018, and it rewards visitors who want to see a fuller, more community-oriented side of an artist mostly known for photographing herself alone in the landscape.

venue.name: The Huntington Library, Art Museum, and Botanical Gardens

shows.title: Venerated
shows.dates_note: Venue's Galleries homepage lists this as its current exhibition with no closing date given; the artist's own site records an opening reception of March 5, 2026, but the gallery page still presents the show as current as of September 2026.
shows.description:
Mark Steven Greenfield has spent five decades reworking the visual language of Christian icon painting — gold leaf, halos, devotional gaze — to canonize Black historical figures whom official history mostly left out. "Venerated" extends his ongoing Halo series with new gold-leaf-and-acrylic panels on wood, each one a portrait-sized "icon" of a resistance leader, folk saint, or survivor drawn from the 1400s through the 1800s.

The individual paintings are modest in scale, roughly 20 by 16 inches, but the iconographic treatment gives each subject an outsized presence: Francisco Manicongo, prosecuted by the Portuguese Inquisition in 1591 in what the gallery describes as the first legal action in the Americas targeting gender nonconformity, appears alongside other figures whose stories connect directly to today's fights over transgender rights, reproductive rights, and voting rights.

Greenfield, an L.A. native who studied under Charles White at Otis and later ran the Watts Towers Arts Center, has built his reputation on this kind of long game — patiently building bodies of work (Incognegro, Black Madonna, Halo) that use appropriated religious form to force a reckoning with erasure. This is a compact but pointed entry in that project, and the Boone Gallery's small scale suits the intimacy of the paintings.

venue.name: Boone Family Art Gallery, Pasadena City College

shows.title: David Lynch: LA
shows.description:
This is the first showing of David Lynch's photography in his adopted home city since his death in 2025, and Pace has built it around the atmosphere he spent fifty years chasing on film and canvas alike. Five bodies of work from 1979 to 2008 are brought together: the large-scale Figures and Smoke portraits of women mid-exhale, black-and-white nude studies that abstract the body into topography, the layered, blurred Couch Series riffing on the art-historical odalisque, deadpan architectural "portraits" of LA's industrial edges, and the wry Kits photographs documenting disassembled fish, chicken, and duck like model-airplane instructions gone uncanny.

None of this is separate from Lynch the filmmaker — the same eye that composed Eraserhead's stables-era Los Angeles or Mulholland Drive's dream logic is visibly at work in these frames, where smoke, mystery, and psychological unease do a lot of quiet work.
